{"title": "Can saying this abusive word lead to an obscenity case? Supreme Court explains in Tamil Nadu land dispute case", "content": "The Supreme Court on Friday clarified that the use of abusive or vulgar language, no matter how offensive or uncivil, does not by itself amount to the criminal offence of obscenity. The court mentioned such words would attract obscenity provisions only if they are lascivious, appeal to prurient interests and have the tendency to deprave or corrupt those exposed to them, reported Bar and Bench.\nThe ruling came from a Bench comprising Justices Sanjay Karol and Vipul M Pancholi while partly allowing the appeal of a man convicted for obscenity after he used the expressions “motherf****r”, “son of a w***e” and other vulgar expletives during a dispute over land.\n“Let’s be clear, legally, obscenity is not synonymous with ‘vulgarity’, ‘abuse’ or ‘profanity’. Use of mere swear words, profanities and vulgar expletives, however distasteful or uncivil they may be, cannot be equated with obscenity...Words which are merely vulgar or abusive may evoke a feeling of disgust, revulsion or shock, but that by itself does not make them obscene in law,” the Court mentioned.\nThe Supreme Court, however, upheld the man's conviction for causing grievous hurt after finding that he had fractured the complainant's nasal bone with a billhook. At the same time, it reduced his sentence to imprisonment till the rising of the court and ordered him to pay a fine of ₹50,000.\nThe case stemmed from an agricultural land dispute in Tamil Nadu in August 2017. According to the prosecution, the conflict began with an argument between the appellant, Mani, and the complainant's brother-in-law over the property. Two days later, Mani allegedly got into another confrontation with the complainant's nephew over the same issue.\nThe prosecution alleged that when the complainant stepped in, Mani verbally abused him with vulgar expletives and caste-based slurs before returning with a billhook from his house and attacking him. The complainant suffered injuries to his forehead, nose and thumb, and subsequent CT scan findings confirmed a fracture of his nasal bone.\nThe trial court found Mani guilty under Sections 294(b) (obscenity), 326 (grievous hurt) and 506(ii) (criminal intimidation) of the Indian Penal Code, along with provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. Subsequently, the Madras High Court acquitted him of the charges under the SC/ST Act but affirmed his convictions under the IPC.\nMani then challenged the High Court's decision before the Supreme Court.\nWhile examining his conviction for obscenity, the apex court observed that the law does not classify every abusive or vulgar remark as obscene.\nThe Bench said that for words to fall within the ambit of Section 294(b) of the IPC, they must be lascivious, appeal to prurient interests and have the tendency to deprave or corrupt those exposed to them. The court also noted that it must be established that the utterance caused annoyance to others.\nWhile examining the legal principles to the facts of the case, the apex court concluded that, even if the prosecution's allegations were accepted in full, the language allegedly used by Mani amounted only to abusive or vulgar remarks and did not meet the legal threshold for the offence of obscenity.\n“In the present case, during altercation, the appellant allegedly uttered that “Hey Motherf****r! You son of a w***e! Are you coming in support of your elder sister's son? Just f**k off, you ‘Kurutha’ F****r..\" Such words, howsoever abusive, unpalatable or uncivil, do not satisfy the requirement of Section 294(b) IPC… Further, it is nobody’s case that use of such words caused annoyance to others in a public place, which is a mandatory ingredient of the Section,” the Court stated, the report noted.\nThe court also acquitted Mani of the charge of criminal intimidation under Section 506(ii) of the IPC. It observed that the mere use of threatening words during a quarrel does not constitute criminal intimidation unless the prosecution establishes that the accused intended to create fear or coerce the victim into performing, or abstaining from performing, a particular act.\nHowever, the Bench upheld Mani's conviction under Section 326 of the IPC for causing grievous hurt. It noted that the medical records supported the complainant's version that Mani had attacked him with a billhook, causing a fracture to his nasal bone, an injury that clearly qualified as grievous hurt under the law.\nGarvit Bhirani is a journalist based in Gurugram. {"title": "Gujarat tops NITI Aayog's Investment Friendliness Index 2026", "content": "Gandhinagar: Gujarat has secured the top position among India's major States in NITI Aayog's first-ever Investment Friendliness Index 2026, reaffirming its standing as the country's leading investment destination.\nAccording to the release, the State achieved the highest score of 56.6, ahead of Maharashtra (53.7) and Tamil Nadu (53.3), in an assessment of 17 major States. The ranking reflects Gujarat's sustained commitment to creating a transparent, efficient and investor-friendly business environment under the leadership of Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel.\nThe Investment Friendliness Index evaluates States across 84 indicators under eight key pillars, covering every stage of the investment lifecycle from policy and governance to infrastructure, business facilitation and fiscal management, as stated in the release.\nRead more: Gujarat emerges as top state in Niti Aayog's Investment Friendliness Index for states and UTs\niNDEXTb's Single-Window Facilitation, Faster NOCs and Stable Labour Environment Win Investor Confidence\nThe Index identifies Gujarat's policy stability and investor-centric governance as among the State's biggest strengths. The Industrial Extension Bureau (iNDEXTb) provides investors with end-to-end facilitation through its single-window system, making the process of setting up businesses faster, simpler and more transparent.\nThe State also offers a well-defined and time-bound framework for securing statutory approvals and No Objection Certificates (NOCs), enabling projects to move from proposal to implementation with minimal delays.\nThe report further notes that restrictions on strikes in essential services have helped maintain industrial peace, resulting in negligible labour disruptions and providing businesses with a stable and predictable operating environment.\nAccording to the Index, Gujarat's world-class industrial infrastructure continues to be one of the State's strongest competitive advantages. Industrial hubs such as Dholera Special Investment Region (SIR), GIFT City, Sanand, Dahej, Jhagadia and Saykha offer world-class plug-and-play facilities, allowing industries to establish operations quickly and efficiently. This integrated industrial ecosystem has significantly improved project execution timelines while reducing the time and cost involved in setting up new businesses.\nThe report also highlights the role of the Vibrant Gujarat Global Summit, which has consistently attracted large domestic and international investment commitments and strengthened Gujarat's position as a global investment destination.\nGujarat has also performed exceptionally well in logistics and connectivity. The State accounts for nearly 10% of India's State highway network, almost four times the national average. It has the country's highest estimated expressway length at 635 kilometres, while nearly 7% of India's railway network passes through the State. Lower turnaround times and efficient logistics have further enhanced supply chain competitiveness.\nThe Index recognises Gujarat's power sector as another major strength supporting industrial growth. Industrial consumers in Gujarat benefit from electricity tariffs that are nearly 29% lower than the national average. The State also provides an average of 23.8 hours of power supply every day, exceeding the average among major States.\nCompetitive electricity tariffs, coupled with reliable power availability, have helped industries lower operating costs while improving productivity and business efficiency.\nThe report highlights Gujarat's strong economic fundamentals as a key factor behind sustained investor confidence. The State contributes 31% of India's total merchandise exports and recorded the third-highest GSDP growth among States during FY 2019-24.\nGujarat's per capita GSDP stands at ₹2,64,232, nearly 67% higher than the average of major States. The report also notes that Gujarat has one of the country's strongest MSME ecosystems, supported by a healthy share of Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs), providing a resilient foundation for industrial growth.\nRead more: Gujarat tops NITI's investment friendliness index; Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu follow\nThe State's fiscal discipline further strengthens its investment credentials. In FY 2024, Gujarat recorded a fiscal deficit of just 2.81% of GSDP, the lowest among all States. Outstanding liabilities stand at around 18% of GSDP, nearly 40% lower than the average of major States, reflecting prudent financial management and long-term economic stability.\nThe Index also acknowledges Gujarat's growing innovation ecosystem as an important driver of future industrial growth. As of FY 2025, the State has established 614 Atal Tinkering Labs (ATLs). With 1.24 ATLs per one lakh population, Gujarat performs nearly 19% above the average of major States, strengthening the ecosystem for innovation, entrepreneurship and emerging technologies.\nAccording to the release, the State achieved the highest score of 56.6, ahead of Maharashtra (53.7) and Tamil Nadu (53.3), in an assessment of 17 major States. {"title": "The tactical evolution that has Spain one win from FIFA World Cup glory", "content": "A month ago, when the World Cup got underway, Spain were among the favourites, though barely anyone was talking about them. Most of the pre-tournament chatter centred on France's frontline, Argentina defending their title, and whether this might be the last World Cup for \nLionel Messi or \nCristiano Ronaldo.\nSpain just got on with it. A goalless draw against Cape Verde in the opener did nothing to change that narrative. Since then, though, this has been one of the most complete tactical campaigns of the tournament: top of Group H, a single goal conceded across the knockout rounds, and a 2-0 dismantling of France in the semi-final that leaves them one win away from a second World Cup title.\n Beyond tiki-taka\nFor the best part of two decades, Spain have meant one thing: tiki-taka. Endless possession, short passing triangles, patience bordering on suffocation. It was the defining feature of the greatest generation this country has produced.\nThis side plays differently. Luis de la Fuente hasn't abandoned the old principles of control through the ball, but he's cut away the predictability that came with them. There's more verticality now, more aggression, more urgency to the passing.\nIt isn't a new development so much as a return, and the numbers trace it clearly. \nAt the 2018 World Cup, where Spain went out on penalties in the last 16, their share of progressive passes sat at 0.82 times the tournament average. In 2022, another round-of-16 exit on penalties, it had dropped further, to 0.76. Then the turn: at Euro 2024, which Spain won, that figure rose to 1.08 times the field average. Now, in this World Cup final, it sits at 1.09. Both exits came in below the average. Both the European champions and the World Cup finalists have sat above it.\nOliver Kahn, the former Germany goalkeeper and Zee5 expert, thinks that shift explains most of what's happened this summer.\n\"They further developed tiki-taka in the last 10 or 12 years. Luis de la Fuente has made some adaptations. They are playing more vertically and much more aggressively, with both full-backs always attacking. This is a totally different Spain than it was 10 years ago.\"\nRobbie Fowler, the former England striker and fellow Zee5 expert, put it similarly in a media session.\n\"Everyone goes on about tiki-taka, and I don't think this is the tiki-taka of Spain that we've seen in the past. They are still a possession-based team, but what I love is it's possession in the right way, it's possession in the right spaces. There's a purpose to how they play.\"\nSpain didn't stop France. Michael Olise had been one of the tournament's sharpest creators. France's expected goals per game had averaged 2.4 through the tournament; against Spain it fell to 0.31, their lowest figure of the summer. Spain allowed them 0.6 xG and generated 1.7 of their own, on a night that was built more around control than chance creation.\nFrance's whole approach through the tournament had relied on winning the ball back and going vertical immediately, exploiting the space behind defences with raw pace. The moment France won possession, Rodri, Fabian Ruiz and Dani Olmo were already closing the passing lanes before Les Bleus could get up any speed. Mbappe spent most of the evening chasing long balls that never quite arrived. Dembele was cut off from the game. Olise, usually France's creative pulse, had his quietest night of the tournament. Mbappe didn't register a single shot on target all match. France managed 10 attempts in total, despite 152 touches in the attacking third.\nA defence that's gone under the radar\nSpain's attacking play tends to get the headlines. The back four deserve just as much attention, maybe more.\nPedro Porro, Pau Cubarsi, Aymeric Laporte and Marc Cucurella have, hands down, become one of the strongest defensive units in the tournament. Across the knockout stage, Spain have conceded a combined 1.59 expected goals, which is a remarkable number for a team that has gone this deep.\nAgainst France specifically, Porro, Rodri, Laporte, Cubarsi and Ruiz won 25 of 34 individual duels and made 44 defensive actions between them. And they didn't break shape to do it.\nBut perhaps the biggest reason behind Spain's success is the one few are talking about: Rodri.\nHe's come back from a difficult club season, one shaped by the serious knee injury he suffered in September 2024, and found something close to his best form exactly when his country needed it. Against France, attacks kept running into him, whether he was intercepting a pass, mopping up loose possession, or simply slowing the game down when Spain needed a breath.\nThe numbers back it up. Rodri has completed 655 passes at this World Cup, more than any player has managed in a single edition since records began in 1966. It's not just a possession stat; it says something about how much of Spain's rhythm runs through one man.\nKahn frames it as a system built to work because the individuals inside it are exceptional.\n\"They have a perfect system, but you always need outstanding guys like Rodri and Lamine.\"\nAlongside Fabian Ruiz and Dani Olmo, Rodri simply outplayed Adrien Rabiot and Aurelien Tchouameni in midfield, and France never found a way back into that battle.\nEven when Didier Deschamps threw on Desire Doue, Manu Kone and Rayan Cherki looking for a way back into the game, Spain just adjusted their pressing triggers and stayed compact. Five matches, one goal, no assists, a long way off the 24 goals and 17 assists he racked up for Barcelona this season.\nThe numbers don't tell you much, though.\nHis running alone forced Lucas Digne into the foul that gave Spain their penalty and their lead against France. Across the tournament he's stretched defences, driven the ball into deep areas, and put opponents on the back foot just by being on the pitch.\nKahn thinks his role with Spain is simply different to the one he plays at club level.\n\"Lamine was coming back from an eight-week injury. Everyone on the pitch seems to know when to press, when to sit back into shape, when to break forward.\nFowler sees it as possession with a purpose behind it, rather than possession as an end in itself.\n\"They still play possession-based football, but I think there's more directness. His expected goal rate has doubled, from 0.26 per 90 minutes four years ago to 0.52 now, and his shot volume and final-third receptions are up to match. {"title": "Declan Rice enters World Cup history books after breaking 90-year-old record with first World Cup goal", "content": "Declan Rice etched his name into both England and FIFA World Cup history after scoring the fastest goal of his international career during England's remarkable 6-4 victory over France in the 2026 World Cup third-place playoff.\nThe England captain struck after just 2 minutes and 14 seconds in Miami to score his first-ever World Cup goal, setting the tone for one of the most extraordinary matches in tournament history. Faced with an oncoming goalkeeper, he calmly slotted a low, composed finish into the bottom corner. After being dropped from the starting lineup in the immediate build-up to the World Cup by manager Thomas Tuchel, his spot was heavily questioned. Promotional campaigns featured Croatian midfielder Luka Modric, legendary former Real Madrid manager José Mourinho, and Argentina's national football team. The company released an advertisement featuring actor Timothée Chalamet in June, when he was drawing attention for his appearances at New York Knicks games during the NBA Finals. Another campaign starring Colombian music artist J Balvin debuted earlier this month.\nDespite the strong momentum, Kalshi's rapid expansion comes as prediction markets face mounting regulatory scrutiny in the United States. Several states argue that sports-event prediction contracts function similarly to sports betting, an area traditionally regulated by state authorities.\nKalshi, however, maintains that prediction markets fall under the jurisdiction of the federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), which oversees derivatives and swap markets. The company supports the federal government's view that the CFTC has exclusive authority to regulate such contracts.\nMansour dismissed criticism from state regulators, arguing that opposition largely comes from established gambling operators concerned about increased competition from prediction market platforms.\nThe company's next challenge will be converting the influx of World Cup users into long-term participants. Trading volumes have already been noticeably lower on days without tournament matches compared with game days.\nStill, Mansour remains optimistic, saying the pattern has repeated itself during previous major events. While activity typically cools once a headline event concludes, new catalysts eventually emerge to drive trading volumes higher again, helping the platform sustain long-term growth.\n“You have to believe there’s not going to be any news after Sunday,” he said. “Maybe, … but the more probable thing is that there’s going to be like a bunch of things going on in the world, and Kalshi’s going to be there to service it.”\nOops! France beat Croatia 4-2 in 2018, while Argentina and France tied 3-3 in 2022 (before Argentina prevailed in a penalty shootout).\nTeams scoring at least two goals have won the World Cup title 17 times; there have been eight instances of a team scoring at least two goals in the final and still falling short.\nThere have been three 1-0 wins: West Germany over Argentina in 1990, Spain over Netherlands in 2010 and Germany over Argentina in 2014. And there was one 0-0 tie in a final; Brazil wound up winning over Italy in a penalty shootout the 1994 final, which had been the only one played on U.S. soil before now.\nBack-to-back championships as coach\nIf Argentina wins on Sunday (July 19, 2026), Lionel Scaloni — who led the team’s push to the 2022 title — would be just the second person to coach two World Cup championship clubs.\nItaly went back-to-back as World Cup champions in 1934 and 1938, with both those clubs coached by Vittorio Pozzo.\nNobody else has two titles as a coach. There are three men — Brazil’s Mário Zagallo, West Germany’s Franz Beckenbauer and France’s Didier Deschamps — to have won World Cups as both a player and a coach.\nMilestones for Messi\nWhen he takes the field Sunday (July 19, 2026), Argentina star Lionel Messi will be the oldest field player to appear in a World Cup final.\nMessi is 39. Sweden’s Gunnar Gren was 37 when he played against Brazil in the 1958 final.\nThe only player older than Messi to play in a final was Italy goalkeeper Dino Zoff — who was 40 when his club beat West Germany for the 1982 crown. Pelé was 17 when he helped Brazil win the final over Sweden in 1958, Giuseppe Bergomi was 18 when Italy beat West Germany in 1982, and Kylian Mbappé was 19 when France beat Croatia in 2018.\nArgentina and Spain’s winning record\nSpain is 28-0-9 in its last 37 matches, which has tied Italy for the longest unbeaten run by a European men’s national team.\nItaly also went 28-0-9 from October 2018 through September 2021 — before losing to Spain 2-1 on Oct. 6, 2021 in Milan.\nArgentina has a streak worth noting as well. It has won seven consecutive World Cup matches, tied with Italy for the second-longest such run in men's tournament history. Only Brazil, which won 11 straight spanning 2002 and 2006, has a longer World Cup winning streak.\nThe game is just the second head-to-head meeting in a World Cup between Argentina and Spain. Argentina won 2-1 in the 1966 group stage.\nAcross all competitions and friendlies, the sides have played 14 times. {"title": "India joins WTO fisheries subsidies pact, backs sustainable fishing", "content": "India has joined the World Trade Organization (WTO) Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies (AFS), the government announced on Monday.\nThe formal acceptance was handed over by Rajesh Agrawal, India’s commerce secretary to Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, the director-general of the WTO in Geneva.\nThe decision reaffirms India's commitment to sustainable fisheries management while preserving marine resources as a source of food security, livelihoods and employment for coastal communities, according to a statement issued by the ministry of commerce and industry.\nIndia has become the 123rd WTO member to formally accept the agreement.\nThe pact focuses on subsidies related to marine wild-capture fishing and fishing-related activities at sea. Aquaculture and inland fisheries remain outside its scope.\nAccording to the ministry, joining the agreement enhances India's credibility as a responsible seafood exporter and supports better access to premium global markets that increasingly value sustainability and traceability.\nThe agreement seeks to protect the livelihoods of traditional and small-scale fishers by promoting sustainable fisheries.\nIt prohibits subsidies linked to illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, as well as fishing of overfished stocks, helping curb unsustainable fishing practices that threaten marine resources while safeguarding the long-term interests of traditional and small-scale fishing communities.\nThe framework is particularly beneficial for countries such as India, where fisheries are predominantly small-scale and the country is not a major participant in industrial fishing.\nAt the same time, the predominance of aquaculture-based shrimp in India's seafood exports—which falls outside the scope of the agreement—ensures the continued resilience and competitiveness of the country's seafood export sector.\nThe WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies is the first multilateral WTO agreement with an environmental sustainability objective.\nIt was adopted by consensus at the 12th WTO Ministerial Conference in Geneva in June 2022. The agreement prohibits government support for illegal fishing activities and the overexploitation of fish stocks, contributing to the protection of marine ecosystems.\nThe agreement entered into force on 15 September 2025 after being accepted by two-thirds of WTO members.\nIndia already has a robust fisheries management framework, strengthened through the Sustainable Harnessing of Fisheries in the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) Rules, 2025, and the Guidelines for Sustainable Harnessing of Fisheries in the High Seas by Indian-Flagged Fishing Vessels, 2025.\n\"India's acceptance of the Agreement reflects its commitment to sustainable fisheries management and responsible marine resource governance. India's domestic fisheries management framework is in alignment with the Agreement and safeguards the interests of traditional and small-scale fishers while contributing to global efforts to promote sustainable fisheries. Above all, by becoming a party to this Agreement, India reinforces its unwavering commitment to the rules-based trading system with the WTO at its core,\" said the commerce ministry in a statement.\nOops! {"title": "RBI Deputy Governor Swaminathan J asks regulated entities to review internal grievance redressal processes", "content": "Mumbai, RBI Deputy Governor Swaminathan J has asked all regulated entities to review their internal grievance redressal processes and design complaint management systems to prevent complaints from inadvertently bypassing the Internal Ombudsman process.\nIn his keynote address at the Internal Ombudsman Conference organised by the RBI on July 13, the deputy governor said that at the heart of banking and financial services lies a fundamental relationship between the customer and institution.\n\"Customers entrust financial institutions with their savings, their aspirations, their financial security and, increasingly, their digital lives.\n\"That relationship is sustained not only by strong balance sheets, adequate capital and advanced technology, but also by how fairly and promptly institutions respond when something goes wrong,\" he said.\nAlso read: RBI asks banks to clear old trade and payment mismatches\nThe Reserve Bank of India (RBI) posted the speech on its website on Monday.\nOver the years, Swaminathan said the Reserve Bank has not only consistently emphasised that consumer protection is integral to financial stability, but has also translated this principle into a comprehensive institutional framework through the RBI Ombudsman mechanism, the Internal Ombudsman framework and robust regulatory expectations for customer service.\nTogether, this framework reflects the RBI's belief that a financial system can be considered truly strong when customers are confident that their concerns will be heard, examined impartially and resolved within a reasonable time.\n\"Every unresolved grievance carries a cost. It is not merely a financial cost. It is a cost in terms of customer confidence, institutional reputation and, ultimately, regulatory attention,\" he said.\nMore importantly, it represents a missed opportunity for the institution to demonstrate fairness, responsiveness, and accountability, the deputy governor emphasised.\nHe further said an effective Internal Ombudsman framework depends on the environment created by the Board and the regulated entity's senior management.\n\"The Board sets the tone for the organisation. If customer-centricity is viewed merely as a compliance requirement, the grievance redress mechanism will inevitably become a compliance exercise,\" Swaminathan said.\nOn the other hand, when the Board views customer service as an integral part of good governance, that philosophy permeates the organisation and reflects in every interaction with the customer.\nThe Board and its Customer Service Committee should, therefore, not view complaint data merely as statistics or management information, he said.\nComplaint trends are valuable business intelligence, he said, adding that rising complaints in a particular product, geography, delivery channel or process often serve as early warning signals of underlying weaknesses that require management attention.\n\"It is observed that a significant proportion of complaints ultimately resolved in favour of customers at the RBI Ombudsman level were not referred to the Internal Ombudsman in the first place. This is a matter of serious concern because it undermines the very purpose of the Internal Ombudsman framework,\" he said.\nSwaminathan urged all the regulated entities to review their internal grievance redress processes carefully.\n\"Every complaint that must be referred to the Internal Ombudsman should be referred promptly and without exception. Equally important, complaint management systems should be designed to prevent complaints from inadvertently bypassing the Internal Ombudsman process due to classification issues or process deficiencies,\" he said.\nHe also highlighted that technology has transformed financial services in ways that would have been difficult to imagine even a decade ago. Technology has undoubtedly enhanced convenience and expanded access to formal finance.\nAlso read: RBI imposes penalties on Muthoot Finance, 5 others for compliance violations\nAt the same time, {"title": "India invites applications for car import quota under India-UK trade pact", "content": "New Delhi, India on Monday invited the first round of applications for the allocation of 2026 import quotas for fully-built passenger cars and goods vehicles under the duty concession provisions of the India-UK free trade agreement.\nUnder the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which came into effect from July 15, New Delhi has allowed the import of a total of 3.78 lakh units of conventional-engine passenger cars, including those in the mass segment, from the UK at a concessional customs duty during the first 15 years of the implementation of the trade pact between the two countries.\nALSO READ | India-UK trade deal: Luxury cars get cheaper, but your Scotch will have to wait\nUnder the pact, tariffs on automotive imports will fall from about 110 per cent to 10 per cent, with quotas on both sides.\nImporters seeking to import vehicles from the UK under the quota-based duty concessions (tariff rate quota - TRQ) provided under the agreement can submit their applications from July 21 to August 4, the directorate general of foreign trade (DGFT) said in a notification.\n\"New applications for TRQ under India - United Kingdom CETA for CY 2026 are invited from July 21, 2026 up to August 04, 2026,\" it said.\nAs per the notification, the applications have been invited for allocation of quota to the importers for 9,316 units in the first phase.\nOnly Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), dealers and channel partners duly authorised by the OEMs of vehicles originating in the UK will be eligible to apply for the Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ).\nTo be eligible, each applicant will submit a pre-purchase agreement issued by an OEM of the vehicles originating in the UK setting out the quantity of vehicles agreed to be supplied to the applicant during the TRQ year for importation into India under each TRQ.\nThe quota for cars with an engine capacity of up to 1,500 cc has been kept at 2,329 units. {"title": "RBI issues draft for future-ready rules related to foreign investments", "content": "Mumbai: The Reserve Bank on Tuesday proposed simplified and future-ready rules related to foreign investments, including those pertaining to overseas listing of Indian companies.\nThe planned revisions in Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules follow Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman's announcement in the Union Budget 2026-27 to carry out a comprehensive review of the rules.\nForeign investment into India is presently governed by the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 ('NDI Rules').\nAlso Read: PLI schemes attract ₹2.4 lakh crore investments, create over 14 lakh jobs till March 2026\nPursuant to the announcement, the Centre other stakeholders, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said it has prepared a draft of the rationalised rules.\nOne of the salient features of the proposed draft rules is a simplified and principle-based framework, the RBI said.\nIt aims to rationalisation of provisions, harmonisation of definitions and a simplified regulatory architecture to enhance clarity and reduce regulatory complexity.\nAlso Read: Gratuity, leave encashment not part of CIRP cost: NCLAT\nAlignment with the FDI policy, enhanced ease of doing business, and a future-ready regulatory framework are other key features, the existing shareholders on a foreign stock exchange, subject to certain conditions.\nOne of the conditions is that the equity should be denominated in INR in the books of the company and held in dematerialised form.\n\"If such company is listed on a recognised stock exchange in India, then issue or offer of equity shall additionally be in compliance with the applicable SEBI regulations and such equity shall rank pari passu with equity listed on a recognised stock exchange in India,\" it said.\nIn case, the company is not listed on a recognised stock exchange in India, then issue or offer of equity should be in compliance with the conditions or requirements prescribed by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.\nThe draft also said that in case of initial listing of equity by a public company which is not listed on a recognised stock exchange in India, the price for issue or transfer of equity would be determined by a book-building process as permitted by the concerned international stock exchange.\nThe draft further said a person resident outside India or an foreign controlled entity (FCE) may make foreign investment on repatriation or non-repatriation basis, by way of subscription to an issue, purchase from any person or gift between natural persons.\nIt also said an NRI or an OCI may subscribe to the National Pension System governed and administered by {"title": "PPI vs WPI: What is Producer Price Index and why will it replace Wholesale Price Index in India?", "content": "The change, more than two decades in the making, will eventually require businesses to rethink how they price and index contracts. \"Businesses should not wait until the formal replacement of WPI by PPI to reassess their contractual frameworks,\" said DK Srivastava, Chief Policy Advisor, EY India.\nAlso read: India introduces PPI for goods and services, begins shift from WPI\nWhat is WPI, and what is PPI?\nAccording to the Ministry's official release, the WPI measures price changes for goods at the wholesale stage. PPI, meanwhile, measures prices received by producers at the point of production, before wholesale margins and taxes are added.To put it simply: consider a packet of biscuits. The PPI is the price the factory receives at the point of production. The WPI tracks its price a step later, when it enters bulk wholesale trading. The CPI, further down the line, is what you finally pay at the retail shop.\nThe Ministry says PPI has three components:\n- Output PPI (OPPI): The prices producers receive for their output.\n- Input PPI (IPPI): The prices producers pay for inputs, currently limited to manufacturing, and released on a trial basis.\n- Service PPI (SPPI): Prices for services, starting with seven sectors, banking, securities transactions, insurance, pension fund management, railways, air passenger transport and telecom.\nAlongside launching PPI, the Ministry also revised WPI's base year to 2022-23 from 2011-12 and expanded its basket from 697 to 957 items, according to the official release.\nSolar, wind and nuclear power have been added under electricity, and crude petroleum and natural gas have been moved from \"primary articles\" to \"fuel and power\" for cleaner classification.\nWhy is WPI being replaced?\nIndia has long relied on two indices to track inflation: WPI, which measures prices at the wholesale stage, and the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which measures what consumers pay.The missing piece, according to the government, has always been the price at the factory gate: what producers themselves receive or pay for goods and services. PPI is designed to fill that gap.\nThe WPI framework also excludes the services sector, even though services now account for more than half of India's economy.\nThe government has said the shift brings India in line with the practice followed by advanced economies such as the US, UK, EU, Japan and China, and with methodology recommended by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).\nWhat are the implications, and what changes?\nPPI is not replacing WPI overnight. According to the release, both indices will run in parallel for five years before WPI is discontinued, giving businesses and government departments time to adjust.The transition matters most for contracts. The Ministry notes that WPI is currently the reference point for indexation, cost escalation and contract pricing across industries, directly affecting cash flows, tariff revisions and risk-sharing between parties. That is why the five-year transition window exists.\nSrivastava added that businesses should use this window to compare both indices and begin recalibrating escalation clauses, particularly in new and long-term contracts. Key risks flagged during the transition include possible mismatches between WPI and PPI trends, friction in renegotiating existing contracts, and the need for reliable historical benchmarks.\nPPI's role also extends beyond inflation tracking. It has already begun feeding into the Index of Industrial Production (IIP), and the government is preparing to use it to deflate nominal output while estimating real GDP, with a revised back-series expected in August.\nAlso read: Govt to replace WPI with Producer Price Index for future procurement contracts\nAccording to Dipti Deshpande, Principal Economist, Crisil, WPI and CPI are currently both used to deflate prices for GDP estimation, and PPI, being a closer measure of producer-level prices, is expected to take over that role over time.\nInput PPI remains on a trial basis for now. The Ministry has said this is deliberate, meant to test data quality and gather feedback from stakeholders before it becomes a full, policy-grade index, meaning that further refinements in coverage and methodology are likely as more data becomes available.", "link": "https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/economy/indicators/ppi-vs-wpi-what-is-producer-price-index-and-why-will-it-replace-wholesale-price-index-in-india/articleshow/132528764.cms", "date": "2026-07-22"}

{"title": "Initiative launched to create Campus Biodiversity Registers across colleges, unversities in India", "content": "Nature Conservation Foundation (NCF), a Mysuru-based wildlife research and conservation organisation, and the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) have launched an initiative to document biodiversity found within college and university campuses across India.\nThe objective of the year-long nationwide exercise is to create a Campus Biodiversity Register (CBR) for each higher education institution.\nAccording to the NCF, the CBR has been inspired by the People’s Biodiversity Register (PBR), which contains comprehensive information on locally available bio-resources, including the landscape and demography of a particular area, and traditional knowledge.\n“The CBR project enables educational institutions to document the biodiversity found within their campuses. While the PBRs document the biodiversity of villages, towns, and cities, the focus of the CBRs is on educational institutions, bringing together students, faculty, and other staff to explore nature around them,” a statement from the organisation said.\nConservationists have underlined the importance of college and university campuses as green spaces in India’s expanding urban landscape. Many such institutions harbour a diversity of trees, birds, butterflies, insects, reptiles, mammals, fungi, and countless other organisms.\n“These campuses often serve as biodiversity hotspots and refuges within urban landscapes, yet surprisingly little is known about the species they support. Without this knowledge, it is difficult to appreciate, conserve and manage these valuable ecosystems,” the statement read.\nThe organisation said colleges and universities can register for the initiative until November 2026, and the documentation will be concluded in June 2027.\nSpecific platforms\nOver the course of a year, participating institutions will document biodiversity using the recognised platforms iNaturalist, eBird, and SeasonWatch. “Whether through organised biodiversity surveys, campus walks, or everyday observations, participants will record the plants, animals, fungi, and other life forms they encounter. By the end of the project, each institution will have the information, skills and resources needed to compile its own CBR,” the NCF said.\nThe biodiversity observations generated through the project are envisaged to contribute to global biodiversity databases while also helping institutions better understand and manage their own campuses. The initiative also aims to foster curiosity about the natural world and encourage a deeper connection between students and the biodiversity that surrounds them.\n“This is an opportunity to notice the biodiversity that often goes unnoticed geckos on classroom walls, moths around campus lights, ants around us, and countless other organisms that quietly share our campuses,” NCF’s programme manager Devica Ranade said on Tuesday (July 21, 2026).\nNBA Chairperson Virendra Tiwary said India’s youth have a crucial role in fulfilling the nation’s commitment to conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity. “Documenting the biodiversity around them is the first step towards conservation,” he said.\nPublished - July 22, 2026 08:28 am IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/energy-and-environment/initiative-launched-to-create-campus-biodiversity-registers-across-colleges-unversities-in-india/article71249558.ece", "date": "2026-07-22"}

{"title": "He couldn’t find anyone to fund his movie. Now this Adivasi filmmaker has won a National Film Award", "content": "Growing up in a small Adivasi hamlet in Jharkhand’s East Singhbhum district, Ravi Raj Murmu remembers evenings when stories travelled not through books or television but through the voices of elders. Parents and grandparents narrated Santhali folktales, stories of bonga (spirits), forests, rivers and unseen worlds, keeping alive an oral tradition that has shaped generations of Adivasi communities.\nYears later, one of those stories has carried Murmu to India’s highest cinematic stage.\nMurmu (33), a Santhal filmmaker from Jharkhand, has won the Best Debut Film of a Director at the 72nd National Film Awards for his 12-minute Santhali short film, Angen, whose title loosely translates as “invisible”, “unseen” or “vanished”. While there is no direct English equivalent, Murmu says the word evokes something that exists but gradually slips out of sight.\n The film travelled through several festivals, including the Mumbai International Film Festival, before finding national recognition. (screenshot)\nThe recognition is significant. Angen is the first Santhali-language film to win a National Film Award and only the second fiction film made in an Adivasi language to be recognised at the stage. The first was Edpa Kana (Going Home), a Kurukh-language short film by Oraon filmmaker Niranjan Kujur, which won the Best Audiography award at the 63rd National Film Awards in 2016. Earlier National Award-winning films by Adivasi filmmakers had been made in Hindi.\nFor Murmu, the award is less about personal recognition than about the stories he has always wanted to tell. “Every story I write comes from Jharkhand,” he said. “They are rooted in Adivasi life. At one point, I realised that if I wanted to make those films honestly, I had to return home.”\nAfter completing his schooling in his village, Murmu studied Mass Communication in Jamshedpur before joining the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII), Pune, where he specialised in editing from 2016 to 2019. He later worked in Mumbai on projects for OTT platforms, including Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and JioCinema, as well as advertising films.\n Beyond its mythical narrative, Angen reflects on the changing relationship between Adivasi-Indigenous people and their connected roots with nature. (screenshot)\nBut despite working in the mainstream industry, he found himself returning to the stories of his childhood. “I realised our own stories have immense strength,” he said. “For a long time we grew up watching other people’s stories. I wanted Santhali cinema to tell its own story.”\nOriginally conceived as a feature-length film that Murmu has been writing for nearly seven years, Angen eventually took the form of a short film after he struggled to secure funding. “A feature would need an investment of around Rs 25-30 crore,” he said. “Since I couldn’t find producers, I decided to make a short film first to show people what the larger story could become.”\nThe film travelled through several festivals, including the Mumbai International Film Festival, before finding national recognition.\nAdapted from a Santhali folktale, Angen follows Sukku, a flute player whose music enchants a goddess living in the spirit world. Drawn into her realm through water, which serves as a portal between the human and spiritual worlds, Sukku later realises he no longer belongs there and begins searching for his village.\n“The search never truly ends,” Murmu said, adding that he deliberately leaves the film open-ended because the larger feature is still being developed.\nBeyond its mythical narrative, Angen reflects on the changing relationship between Adivasi-Indigenous people and their connected roots with nature. The movie quietly captures how rapid urbanisation reshapes landscapes once associated with Adivasi spiritual life.\nThrough metaphor, the film shows how, as urbanisation expands, forests disappear, natural spaces shrink, and even those spiritual spaces begin to vanish.\nWater in the movie, Murmu said, was chosen consciously. “Science tells us life began with water. That’s why I made water the medium through which one world connects to another,” he said.\nThe title too carries layered meanings, he said. “There is no literal translation of Angen,” he said. “You can call it invisible, vanished or unseen, but none of those words fully express what it means.”\nThe idea to show the disappearing world of Adivasis came after a visit home from Pune. Arriving at the Galudih bus stand near his village, Murmu failed to recognise the place after new infrastructure had transformed the landscape. “That made me realise how quickly places change,” he said. “If we don’t document our stories now, many of them may disappear.”\nMade on a modest budget with the support of friends and theatre artists, the film stars NSD graduate Jitray Hansda as the older Sukku, Ramchandran Mardi as the younger Sukku and Saloni Soren in the lead female role.\n“I worked with the people who believed in the project,” Murmu said. “Without them, this film wouldn’t have been possible.”\nEven as Angen earns national recognition, Murmu has already resumed work on his first feature film, with shooting expected to begin soon.\nFor an Adivasi filmmaker who grew up listening to stories around village homes, the journey from oral tradition to the National Film Awards marks more than a personal milestone. “It is also a reminder that Adivasi stories in their languages, long confined to memory and folklore, are now finding a place on India’s biggest cinematic stage… this is why representation matters,” he said.", "link": "https://indianexpress.com/article/india/angen-national-film-award-ravi-raj-murmu-first-santhali-film-winner-10796628/", "date": "2026-07-22"}

{"title": "FIFA World Cup 2026 | Spain refines its style, rekindles winning spree", "content": "Argentina had won its previous three major tournaments — two Copa Americas on either side of the 2022 FIFA World Cup. It had not lost a knockout duel since the 2019 Copa America. It had made fighting back from the brink look like clockwork. It had Lionel Messi, the greatest player of this generation and arguably of all time, in its midst.\nFrance had finished runner-up in the previous World Cup, and roared with unbridled joy in the edition prior to that. It had the most dazzling array of attacking players in Kylian Mbappe, Michael Olise and Ousmane Dembele.\nYet, when they met Spain at the business end of the just-concluded quadrennial spectacle in the United States, Canada and Mexico, neither seemed to turn up. Or more accurately, they were not allowed to turn up.\nALSO READ: FIFA World Cup 2026: A grand spectacle despite its share of controversies\nSuch was the dominance of the Spaniards in North America as they capped off a near-flawless campaign — remarkably, the goalless draw against Cape Verde in their opener was the only stutter in the entire tournament — with a 1-0 win over Argentina in the final to lift their second World Cup.\nMuch like the incandescent march to the title by an elite group of players in 2010, many of whom were in the stands at the New York New Jersey Stadium on Sunday afternoon to watch their countrymen thoroughly outclass Messi’s troops, the Iberian nation’s latest conquest on the grand stage is not merely a victory on the field of play. It is also a renewed vindication of an idea and identity that is rooted in a deep affiliation for keeping the ball.\nThe genesis of it in the Spanish set-up dates back to Luis Aragones’ time as head coach in the mid-2000s. Having overseen Spain’s round-of-16 exit to France at the 2006 World Cup in Germany, the bespectacled tactician paved the way for a course-correction by trading La Furia Roja — a more direct, physical approach — for a possession-based game.\nThat he had midfielders of the ilk of Xavi and Andres Iniesta, who had been schooled in this philosophy at La Masia — Barcelona’s renowned youth academy — and were beginning to come into their own, facilitated a smooth-sailing transition. As intended, Spain found long-awaited success at the 2008 European Championship.\nFor the idea to become the envy of the footballing world, the entry of Pep Guardiola as Barcelona manager in the summer of 2008 was even more significant. With Messi, Xavi, Iniesta and Sergio Busquets among his core contingent, Guardiola elevated that style, modelled on intricate passing, playing out from the back and retaining possession, to another degree. Tiki-taka would become an integral part of the sport’s lexicon and embody the beautiful game in all its glory.\nAt the international level, Vicente del Bosque, who took over from Aragones as Spain coach after Euro 2008, knew better than to veer away from these tried-and-tested tactics. More success inevitably came Spain’s way at the 2010 World Cup and Euro 2012.\nEver since, the importance of keeping the ball has been drilled into Spain’s footballers across all levels from a very early age. Pressing opponents high up the pitch as soon as they lose possession is another ingredient fundamental to this playbook. In a nutshell, no team retains possession better than Spain, and nobody recovers the ball as quickly. That is a surefire way of winning football matches, isn’t it?\nEven so, Spain stagnated and fell into a rut where it didn’t win a lot of World Cup games between 2012 and 2024. In the carnival in Brazil in 2014, the defending champion was jolted by a shock group-stage exit.\nIn 2018 and 2022, it couldn’t advance past the round of 16. In Qatar four years ago, Spain’s manner of defeat to Morocco was particularly jarring, for its ouster via a penalty shootout after a drab 120 minutes was marked by a distinct absence of penetration in the final third. Pass after pass was played without an end product. Spain’s obsession with possession, perhaps rightly, was labelled by its critics as dour and devoid of imagination.\nFew would have anticipated, then, that Luis de la Fuente would be the man to engineer a turnaround. Appointed in December 2022 in the immediate aftermath of a disastrous World Cup that Luis Enrique paid the price for, de la Fuente, 61 then, was barely known beyond his country’s borders.\nMuch to the credit of the federation, what he did have in spades was an intimate understanding of the players he was going to work with. He had played a pivotal part in the development of many of them in his capacity as coach of Spain’s junior teams, winning the U-19 European Championship in 2015 and the U-21 equivalent in 2019. He knew the buttons to press to get the best out of these players.\nInstead of throwing the baby out with the bathwater, de la Fuente shrewdly stuck to the principal identity of Spanish football in the 21st century and embellished it with his own beliefs. Instead of the slow, sometimes monotonous build-up that involved a sequence of short passes in search for the perfect goal, de la Fuente would set up his team to be more fluid in its use of a large share of possession. The former full-back employed greater attacking width, and desired the ball circulating more quickly through the middle of the park.\nBack to being the best\nThe results have been resounding. Having won every game on the way to claiming a record fourth European title in 2024, the Spanish juggernaut stitched together an unbeaten run at this World Cup too.\nIn Sunday’s final, Messi and Co. were a distant second. As is its wont, Spain had 60 percent of possession, and 20 attempts in comparison to Argentina’s two. The Albiceleste’s first shot came during the second half of extra time. Not one was on target.\nSuch supremacy wouldn’t have been possible without the calming, all-encompassing influence of Rodri. Blessed with the passing range of a playmaker and the physicality of a centre-back, the 6’3” defensive midfielder combines the dual responsibility of orchestrating Spain’s attacks and suppressing the rival’s threats with aplomb. As per Opta, the 30-year-old delivered 122 line-breaking passes at this World Cup, the most in a single edition since compatriot Xabi Alonso’s 126 in 2010.\nTo be presented the Golden Ball at the end of Sunday’s final — awarded to the best player of the tournament — was a fitting recognition of his contribution over the past month. If he has a robust beginning to the club season with Manchester City, a second Ballon d’Or could be another feather in an ornate cap by the end of the year.\nALSO READ: Football is simple for complete midfielder Rodri\nDefensive solidity\nThat Spain conceded just a solitary goal in the tournament — against Belgium in the quarterfinals — was also down to goalkeeper Unai Simon and a well-drilled defensive unit. While Simon wasn’t really required to make desperate saves worthy of making the highlight packages, his inclination to step up as a sweeper, a la Germany’s Manuel Neuer from recent memory, enabled Spain’s defence to hold a high line. There were instances in both the semifinal and final when the French and Argentine forwards successfully beat the offside trap and ran behind the defence, but Simon was ever so swift to charge out of the box and clear the danger.\nIn keeping a clean sheet in seven out of eight matches, the precocious Pau Cubarsi also played a sparkling part. All of 19, the centre-back’s positional awareness and reading of the game were well beyond his tender age. It meant that he was one of only two outfield players, the other being left-back Marc Cucurella, to play every minute of the competition for Spain.\nWith such a tightly-knit defensive unit working in tandem, Spain’s forwards were never encumbered with having to chase a game. Not once, in fact, did the European giant trail in its quest for the holy grail, a first in 23 editions cutting across 96 years. The attack wasn’t free-flowing to start with, struggling to get past the gutsy Vozinha in the Cape Verde goal despite enjoying a plethora of possession. It may have invited some doubts about Spain retreating to a turgid style.\nBut once de la Fuente brought a fit-again Lamine Yamal and Dani Olmo into the mix from the get-go in the second game against Saudi Arabia, the dynamism in Spain’s attacking play returned and it romped to a 4-0 win. While Olmo’s foremost strength is his ability to receive the ball on the half-turn and dribble his way through congested spaces, Yamal’s trickery on the right wing is a sight for sore eyes.\nThe wunderkind sparkled in spurts without quite seizing the spotlight as a teenaged Pele did in 1958 or Mbappe in 2018. A torn left hamstring at the back end of a hectic season with Barcelona may have been a factor, but it is instructive of the high regard he is held in that opponents yet felt the need to often double up against the 19-year-old.\nYamal’s scope for growing into a great of the game applies to many of the other members too. Sample the case of Nico Williams. The 24-year-old has pace to burn on the left wing, but circumstances curtailed his impact at this event. One of the breakthrough stars of the Euros two summers ago, Williams came into this year’s marquee competition with a hamstring injury.\nTo compound matters, he suffered a right adductor muscle injury in the final group encounter against Uruguay. Still, he came off the bench and provided the assist for Ferran Torres’ 106th-minute winner in the summit clash.\nThe conclusion of a World Cup, regardless of the outcome, usually marks the end of a cycle. With so many in this champion outfit yet to hit their prime, however, this feels like just the start of a very special era. After winning the World Cup in 2010, the men in bright red had to wait 16 years for a second star to be emblazoned above their crest. The third is likely to come far sooner.\nPublished - July 21, 2026 11:28 pm IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/sport/football/fifa-world-cup-2026-spain-refines-its-style-rekindles-winning-spree/article71250916.ece", "date": "2026-07-22"}
{"title": "Possession with purpose unlocks Spain’s World Cup puzzle", "content": "The oldest footballing lesson in Spain has always been deceptively simple. If you have the ball, the opponent cannot score.\nFor years, however, that philosophy became both its greatest gift and its greatest burden. Spain monopolised possession, accumulated passes and controlled territory, but too often it left tournaments wondering whether beautiful football alone could still win the biggest prizes. The echoes of tiki-taka lingered long after the golden generation had faded, sometimes becoming an identity that imprisoned rather than liberated.\nAt this World Cup, Spain did not abandon its football. It rediscovered its purpose.\nLuis de la Fuente’s world champions finished the tournament with the best defence, conceding only one goal in eight matches. They dominated possession as La Roja always have, but possession was no longer the destination. It became the platform from which every other part of the game flourished. They pressed ferociously when they lost the ball, attacked vertically when spaces opened and defended with a discipline that suffocated some of the world’s finest forwards.\nBy the time Rodri lifted the trophy after the 1-0 victory over Argentina, Spain had beaten Portugal, Belgium, France and the defending champion in successive knockout rounds. There could be little argument about the legitimacy of its crown.\nThe numbers only reinforced what the eye had already seen. France had arrived in the semifinal with the tournament’s most feared attack. Kylian Mbappe, Ousmane Dembele and Michael Olise had combined for 13 goals and 10 assists in their first six matches. Spain reduced them to shadows. Mbappe failed to register a shot on target. France managed only three efforts on target all evening and generated barely 0.15 expected goals from its celebrated front three. Spain’s centre-backs Pau Cubarsi and Aymeric Laporte defended aggressively on the halfway line, while Rodri and Fabian Ruiz erased passing lanes before danger could develop.\nALSO READ: Football is simple for complete midfielder Rodri\nAgainst Belgium in the quarterfinals, Spain patiently waited until Mikel Merino struck the decisive late winner. Against Portugal, it accepted a tactical battle and found the goal required to make it past the Iberian neighbours. In the final, it denied Lionel Messi the fairytale ending that seemed almost scripted.\nEvery challenge demanded something different and Spain always had an answer.\nThat adaptability perhaps best explains why this team succeeded where previous Spanish sides had fallen. The Spain of Vicente del Bosque often appeared convinced that enough possession would eventually solve every problem. De la Fuente’s Spain understood that football offers many different questions.\nSometimes the answer was Lamine Yamal. Still only a teenager, Yamal entered the tournament carrying expectations that would have burdened far older footballers. His acceleration, disguised passing and fearlessness repeatedly tilted matches before opponents had organised themselves. Yet unlike so many young stars, he was never asked to carry Spain alone. Around him functioned a collective that was entirely free of hierarchy.\nRodri remained the team’s metronome, rarely hurried, forever choosing the correct pass before pressure arrived. He has now won the Player of the Tournament both in the Euro and the World Cup. Fabian Ruiz produced perhaps the finest tournament of his career, knitting midfield together while contributing goals and relentless defensive work. Nico Williams stretched defences from the opposite flank whenever he played, while Dani Olmo drifted between lines, creating overloads wherever Spain needed them. Mikel Oyarzabal provided the goals to soothe down the nerves after the initial draw with Cape Verde.\nThe full-backs pushed high enough to create width without exposing the defence and goalkeeper Unai Simon was called upon surprisingly infrequently, a reflection of how effectively those in front of him protected the penalty boxes. Whenever Spain lost possession, the counter-press arrived almost instinctively, often recovering the ball before opponents could string together three passes.\nEvery attacker defended. Every defender initiated attacks. Possession, pressing and positional discipline became parts of the same movement rather than separate ideas.\nThere was also a maturity that distinguished this side from many previous champions.\nSpain rarely chased matches emotionally. It never seemed rushed by the occasion, whether facing Kylian Mbappe in Dallas, Belgium in Los Angeles or Lionel Messi in the MetLife Stadium. Its football carried the serenity of a team that knew exactly who it was.\nFor much of the past decade, international football has been shaped by transition, athleticism and chaos. Spain reminded everyone that control still matters. But it also demonstrated that control no longer means simply completing 800 passes.\nIt means controlling space, tempo, emotions and ultimately the result.\nIn doing so, de la Fuente’s players achieved something larger than lifting the World Cup. They completed Spanish football’s evolution.\nPublished - July 21, 2026 07:28 pm IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/sport/football/fifa-world-cup/possession-with-purpose-unlocks-spains-world-cup-puzzle/article71249898.ece", "date": "2026-07-22"}
{"title": "FIFA World Cup 2026: A grand spectacle despite its share of controversies", "content": "For six weeks, the country that had spent decades calling football soccer could talk about little else.\nThe game poured into the United States through its airports and railway stations, occupied its downtowns and suburbs, and turned stadium parking lots into temporary republics of colour, song and shared obsession. Argentinians carried their mate through hotel lobbies. Mexicans arrived with sombreros and booming brass bands. Brazilians brought drums, Colombians danced, the English colonised pubs and supporters from countries separated by oceans discovered one another on trains, concourses and pavements.\nIn New York, Philadelphia, Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Dallas, Los Angeles and the other host cities, football was no longer an immigrant game.\nFor one extraordinary summer, it had taken over the American psyche.\nThe US has always possessed the infrastructure for sporting excess: enormous arenas, endless commercial possibilities, a culture fluent in spectacle and a population drawn from nearly every footballing nation on earth. The World Cup brought all those elements together on a scale the tournament had never previously attempted.\nForty-eight nations, 1,039 players and 104 matches featured in the tournament co-hosted by the USA, Mexico and Canada. A record 6,810,966 spectators attended, more than the combined totals of the previous two World Cups in Russia and Qatar. The 16 venues operated at 99.7% capacity, with an average attendance of 65,490.\nThe figures described the tournament’s size. They could not fully capture its presence.\nThere were supporters who crossed continents and families who crossed generations. Fathers who had discovered Argentina through Diego Maradona returned with sons who had fallen in love with Lionel Messi. Children wore the shirts of countries they had never visited. Diaspora communities that usually experienced international football through television suddenly found their teams appearing a short drive away.\nA Brazilian home match could emerge in New Jersey. Argentina could turn Atlanta or Dallas into Buenos Aires for an evening. The Haitians could revel in defeat, while the African diaspora celebrated the march of nine of the continent’s nations into the knockout rounds.\nAmerica did not simply host the world. Much of the world was already living within it.\nThat was why the atmosphere felt different from the carefully imported FIFA spectacle. The passion did not have to be manufactured. It existed in Queens and New Jersey, in South Florida’s Latin American communities, among West Africans in the Washington corridor and South Asians who followed Argentina from one end of the country to the other.\nThey filled the spaces between the matches. They turned hotel breakfasts into fan gatherings, railway platforms into debates and city streets into improvised parades. The World Cup became visible even to Americans who had no ticket and little previous relationship with the sport.\nAnd the football rewarded them.\nSuccess stories\nThe expanded tournament offered concerns about excess, but it also allowed unfamiliar stories to develop alongside the established powers. Cape Verde supplied one of its most romantic journeys. Norway and Erling Haaland eliminated Brazil. Egypt reached the pre-quarterfinals and pushed Argentina to the edge. By the semifinals, the old hierarchy had returned through Spain, Argentina, France and England, but the road towards it had been crowded with resistance.\nThe leading players who arrived with reputations largely lived up to them. Messi extended his World Cup appearance record to 34 matches and, at 39 years and 25 days, became the oldest outfield player to feature in a final. Kylian Mbappe, Haaland, Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham contributed goals and moments worthy of the stage. Rodri controlled the tournament’s decisive matches and was rightly named its finest player, not overshadowed by the glamorous goal-scorers who have a penchant of hogging all the attention.\nSpain’s teenagers offered a glimpse of what might come next. Lamine Yamal and Pau Cubarsí became only the fourth and fifth teenagers to appear in a men’s World Cup final, joining Pele, Giuseppe Bergomi and Mbappe in the exclusive group to have done so and finished as champions. Their eight appearances were also the most played at a World Cup before turning 20.\nThe tournament became a meeting point between football’s past and future. Messi pursued one last title while Yamal began building a legacy of his own.\nThere was entertainment almost everywhere. The 308 goals surpassed the previous tournament record of 172, while the average of 2.96 per game was the highest since the 1970 World Cup in Mexico. Long-range shooting returned as a significant weapon, while late goals repeatedly transformed knockout matches.\nArsene Wenger, FIFA’s chief of global football development, believed the tournament would be remembered for its physical intensity, increased competitive balance and the performances of its biggest stars. Gianni Infantino went considerably further, declaring that the World Cup had not merely broken records but “smashed” and “destroyed” them.\nFIFA rarely misses an opportunity to proclaim its own success.\nBut this was not a flawless tournament.\nThere were moments when football’s American takeover began to resemble football being taken over by America.\nMatches were divided by mandatory three-minute hydration breaks, even in air-conditioned or closed-roof stadiums, creating pauses conveniently suited to television advertising. The final received a Super Bowl-style extended half-time show. Commercial messaging seemed to occupy almost every unclaimed second, leaving traditionalists wondering whether FIFA had discovered new ways to monetise the game’s natural rhythm.\nTicket prices placed many matches beyond the reach of ordinary supporters, even if the stands ultimately remained full. Travel between distant host cities was expensive and exhausting. The scale that made the tournament historic also made it cumbersome.\nThere were more serious concerns around refereeing and VAR. Portugal’s victory over Croatia became an almost continuous video review, with four goals disallowed in a single match. Egypt’s dramatic defeat to Argentina produced accusations of inconsistency after a goal was ruled out, appeals for a late penalty involving Mohamed Salah were rejected and Argentina scored its winner soon afterwards. The Egyptian Football Association formally questioned the fairness and transparency of the officiating.\nArgentina’s quarterfinal against Switzerland brought further arguments over a red-card decision, while a tournament promoted as the most technologically advanced in history often demonstrated that more cameras did not necessarily produce greater agreement.\nBalogun controversy\nNothing damaged that trust more than the case of Folarin Balogun. The US striker was sent off following a VAR review, ordinarily carrying an automatic one-match suspension. But after President Donald Trump telephoned Infantino and publicly intervened, FIFA lifted the ban, allowing Balogun to face Belgium. FIFA argued that its disciplinary committee had independently determined that the offence did not merit suspension, but the optics were devastating.\nBelgium coach Rudi Garcia called it a decision that would hurt both the World Cup and the US. UEFA officials viewed it as a breach of established protocol, while the episode created the impression that football’s laws could be renegotiated through access to political power.\nIt was an uncomfortable reminder that FIFA’s closeness to the American President had become one of the tournament’s persistent subplots.\nThat relationship reached its awkward conclusion during the final presentation.\nAfter Spain defeated Argentina 1-0 in New Jersey, Trump joined Infantino to present the medals and trophy. He was loudly booed by sections of the crowd but remained on the podium after Rodri had received the World Cup, standing prominently among the Spanish players as they started their celebrations.\nThe image was difficult to ignore: a President accustomed to occupying every available camera angle standing beside a team whose greatest moment should have belonged entirely to them.\nFor all FIFA’s excess, the political intrusion, the refereeing arguments and the relentless commercialisation, the tournament demonstrated something long suspected but never previously tested on such a scale.\nThe US is ready for football.\nNot merely for a version of it packaged as occasional entertainment, stripped of its culture and sold between other American sports. It was ready for the full, unruly game: the tribalism and tension, the tactical arguments, the national longing, the heartbreak of elimination and the songs that continued long after the players had left.\nThe country did not suddenly abandon baseball, basketball or American football. Nor did everyone stop calling the game soccer. But for six weeks, the distinction had hardly mattered.\nAmericans learned the names. They debated VAR. They complained about referees. They arranged work and travel around kick-off times. They discovered that a scoreless match could be gripping despite their own sports regularly producing double-triple digit scores.\nThe World Cup came seeking a host. It left with a newfound audience.\nPublished - July 21, 2026 07:15 pm IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/sport/football/fifa-world-cup-2026-a-grand-spectacle-though-not-without-flaws/article71249621.ece", "date": "2026-07-22"}

{"title": "Why are central banks buying more gold? Here's what it means for the global economy", "content": "According to the World Gold Council's (WGC) latest Central Bank Gold Reserves Survey, official institutions have purchased an average of 1,000 tonnes of gold annually over the past four years—roughly double the average annual purchases recorded over the previous decade. The buying spree shows little sign of slowing, with 89% of surveyed central banks expecting global official gold reserves to increase over the next year, while 45% expect to add to their own holdings, a record high.\nThe findings underscore gold's growing role as a strategic reserve asset at a time when the global economy is grappling with geopolitical conflicts, trade tensions and heightened financial market volatility.\nWhy are central banks buying more gold?\nAt the heart of the buying trend is diversification.Central banks typically hold foreign exchange reserves comprising assets such as US Treasury securities, government bonds and foreign currencies to support their own currencies and maintain financial stability. Gold, however, occupies a unique position because it is a physical asset that carries no credit or counterparty risk and cannot be created at will like fiat currencies.\nUnlike paper currencies, whose value can be eroded by inflation or expansionary monetary policies, gold's supply is naturally constrained. That makes it an effective hedge against inflation and a store of value during periods of economic uncertainty.\nThe WGC survey found that reserve managers continue to rank gold's performance during crises, portfolio diversification and inflation hedging among the primary reasons for increasing allocations. Many also cited geopolitical risks and concerns over sanctions as factors reinforcing gold's importance within reserve portfolios.\nAnother attraction is gold's historical tendency to move independently—or even inversely—to the US dollar. Since the dollar still accounts for the largest share of global foreign exchange reserves, holding gold helps reduce concentration risk and cushions reserve portfolios during periods of dollar weakness or heightened market stress.\nWhy are countries bringing gold home?\nThe WGC survey also points to a gradual shift in where central banks choose to store their bullion.While institutions such as the Bank of England and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York remain key global vaulting centres, an increasing number of central banks are opting to keep a larger portion of their reserves domestically.\nRespondents reported storing at least some gold within their own country, up significantly from the previous year, reflecting a growing emphasis on direct control over strategic reserves amid geopolitical uncertainty.\nA structural shift rather than a short-term trade\nThe renewed appetite for gold is widely viewed as a structural shift rather than a tactical investment.Central bank purchases have remained elevated since 2022 despite record-high gold prices, suggesting reserve managers are prioritising long-term financial resilience over short-term price movements. Many expect gold to account for a larger share of global reserves over the coming years, while the share of the US dollar is seen gradually declining, according to the survey.\nFor policymakers, the rationale is straightforward: in an increasingly fragmented global economy marked by geopolitical conflicts, sanctions, volatile currencies and uncertain inflation, gold continues to offer qualities that few other reserve assets can match—liquidity, independence from any single sovereign issuer and the ability to preserve value across economic cycles.", "link": "https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/economy/finance/why-are-central-banks-buying-more-gold-explained/articleshow/132553871.cms", "date": "2026-07-23"}
