{"title": "SEBI, IFSCA-recognised Category I and II AIFs exempted from PAN requirement", "content": "For expeditious onboarding of foreign investors, the Central Board of Direct Taxes has amended the Income Tax rules to exempt various categories of Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), including those located in International Financial Services Centres, from the requirement of a Permanent Account Number (PAN). Experts say this move will also ensure continuity of reforms for foreign investors.\nA notification, dated July 21, provided for substituting a clause in the rule (157) which exempts persons from obtaining a PAN. Now, the clause defines specified fund means any fund established or incorporated in India in the form of a trust, a company, a limited liability partnership or a body corporate which has been granted a certificate of registration as a Category I or Category II Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) and is regulated under SEBI regulations or the International Financial Services Centres Authority (Fund Management) Regulations. Category III AIFs are already exempted.\nUnderstanding the AIF categories\nCategory I AIFs invest in start-up or early-stage ventures, social ventures or SMEs, infrastructure or other sectors or areas which the government or regulators consider as socially or economically desirable. These include venture capital funds, SME Funds, social venture funds, and infrastructure funds. AIFs which do not fall in Category I and III and which do not undertake leverage or borrow other than to meet day-to-day operational requirements.\nThese include various types of funds, such as real estate funds, private equity (PE) funds, distressed asset funds, etc. Category III AIFs are those that employ diverse or complex trading strategies and may use leverage, including through investments in listed or unlisted derivatives. Various types of funds, such as hedge funds and PIPE Funds, are registered as Category III AIFs.\nExperts see faster onboarding for foreign investors\nExperts say the amendment will help with faster onboarding. According to Amit Maheshwari, Managing Partner, AKM Global, by extending the eligibility from the earlier Category III AIFs to Category I and Category II, regulated by SEBI and the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA), the amendment widens the ambit of the existing framework and aligns it with the evolving investment landscape.\nObtaining a PAN has often been viewed by overseas investors, particularly those with passive investments, as an additional compliance requirement. Extending the PAN exemption framework to Category I and Category II AIFs removes a practical bottleneck in fund investments. “This reform should facilitate faster onboarding of foreign investors while enhancing the competitiveness of India’s alternative investment fund ecosystem removing procedural barrier. Collectively, such measures reaffirm the Government’s commitment to fostering a globally competitive fund management ecosystem and strengthening India’s position as an attractive international investment destination,” he said.\nMove seen as ensuring continuity of reforms\nMeanwhile, some experts see the new notification as a continuation of reforms. Richa Sawhney, Partner (Tax) at Grant Thornton Bharat, said that the PAN exemption framework for eligible non-resident investors investing through specified funds existed under the earlier tax regime as well. This notification ensures that investors in Category I and Category II AIFs, including eligible IFSC-based funds, continue to remain covered under the new Rules by expressly including such funds within the definition of ‘specified fund’. “The amendment therefore preserves the existing compliance relief available to investors in these funds and provides continuity and certainty to global investors,” she said.\nPublished on July 22, 2026", "link": "https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/economy/policy/sebi-ifsca-recognised-category-i-and-ii-aifs-exempted-from-pan-requirement/article71253236.ece", "date": "2026-07-23"}

{"title": "India’s rice fields now rank among world’s top methane hotspots", "content": "Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from paddy fields worldwide have doubled since the 1960s, a new study in NatureFood has found. In the most recent decade, 2011-2020, paddy fields around the world produced around 1.1 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent (CO2-e) emissions every year — a 90.4% increase from the annual emissions between 1961 and 1980, the study reported.\nUpon examining the sources contributing to the rise in emissions, the study found that about half the increase was driven by the loss of soil organic carbon. Between 1961 and 1980, paddy fields were soil organic carbon sinks, removing some 289 million tonnes of CO2-e emissions annually. However, the sink weakened over time. In the 2010s, over a third of paddy fields worldwide in fact began losing carbon from the soil.\nApart from soil organic carbon, methane from paddy fields was also a significant driver of emissions. Flooded fields develop low-oxygen conditions where methane-producing microbes thrive. And paddy fields in eastern India were among the global methane hotspots.\n‘Comprehensive assessment’\n“Most previous studies have focused on a single greenhouse gas, a specific management practice or a particular region,” Hanqin Tian, co-author of the study and director and institute professor, Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Boston College, the U.S., said.\n“Our study provides a much more comprehensive assessment by integrating a global meta-analysis of more than 1,200 field experiments, process-based ecosystem modelling, and artificial intelligence approaches to quantify GHG emissions from rice cultivation worldwide.”\nIndia tops the list of countries on rice production, delivering 154 million tonnes in 2025-26. The area under paddy cultivation has also increased by around 25% since the 1970s, and currently covers 55% of India’s rainfed harvested area. This expansion, together with continuous irrigation of fields, incorporating residues such as leftover stalks, leaves, and stubble, and increasing use of nitrogen fertilisers, also increased emissions.\nPaddy fields v. Germany\nConsidering rice’s crucial role in India’s food security, the study underscored the need for urgent measures to reduce emissions while ensuring sustainable production.\n“Our analysis indicates that a combination of improved irrigation, optimised fertiliser use, residue management, and reduced tillage could reduce global rice-related greenhouse gas emissions by about 10% by mid-century, even under a warming climate,” Dr. Tian said.\nThe study also projected that between 2031 and 2050, annual emissions will increase by around 26%, fuelled by global warming, erratic rainfall, and the continued intense use of agricultural inputs.\nIrrigated paddy fields in India release around 3.9 million tonnes of methane every year. This is a little more than the entire annual methane emissions of Germany.\nPotential and incentives\nWhile India has not set up goals to reduce emissions from agriculture, several techniques and incentives are currently available to farmers.\nThe National Innovations in Climate Resilient Agriculture (NICRA) project, for example, suggests the ‘System for Rice Intensification’ technique to reduce emissions. Here, young seedlings are transplanted in a precise manner and fields are not continuously flooded during irrigation. Direct-seeded rice, where rice seeds are directly sown in fields as opposed to the traditional method of cultivation involving the transplantation of seedlings into a flooded field, is also encouraged. Drip Irrigation and the alternate wetting and drying technique — where the fields are only intermittently flooded — are also promoted.\nHowever, they don’t address the fact that the emission reduction potentials vary widely between India’s States. Apart from large-scale demonstrations of these techniques across districts under NICRA, several country and state-level policies, like the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture and financial incentives provided by states like Punjab and Haryana, aim to encourage the adoption of DSR and SRI. However, the reluctance to change from traditional practices, along with issues such as labour shortages, lack of technical knowledge, and changes in rainfall patterns, constrain farmers’ decisions.\nPrakashan Chellattan Veettil, senior agricultural and behavioural economist at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), New Delhi, said a regional approach that considers the topography, soil, and irrigation conditions plus the farmers’ requirements is crucial.\nDr. Veettil is the IRRI lead in the KERA-AWD project, which is working to establish processes to cultivate low-emission rice systems in Kerala’s low-land (Thrissur kole lands) and mid-land (Palakkad Malampuzha canal) regions.\n“Using a multi-pronged approach, which includes increasing soil organic carbon, understanding the hydrology and aligned irrigation systems, agricultural inputs, residue management protocols, soil microbes and farmer preferences, we are working on identifying low-emission packages, where a combination of these factors can help reduce emissions for various paddy varieties,” Dr. Veettil said.\nHe shared the example of lime that farmers use to neutralise the acidic soil that prevails in the State.\n“We have observed that replacing a portion of the lime with [a material called] phosphogypsum has a positive impact on emissions in the subsoil surface,” he added. “We are also experimenting with different formulations and application methods for nitrogen fertilisers.”\nExpansion of paddy\nAshwini Chhatre, associate professor of public policy and executive director at the Bharti Institute of Public Policy, Hyderabad, said that depending on a region’s suitability for paddy, farmers should have support to opt for low-emission techniques or grow alternative local crop varieties. In his research, Dr. Chhatre found that despite facing climate-related losses and price variations, farmers still dedicate large areas of their farmlands to paddy.\n“As a general strategy, there is no way forward without crop diversification,” he said. “Despite the agro-climatic diversity in the country, paddy has the largest area under cultivation at the cost of regional indigenous crops.”\nDr. Chhatre said several traditional millet varieties in Odisha have been replaced with high-yielding paddy. Reports indicate the State’s paddy fields have contributed the most to its greenhouse gas emissions.\nThrough initiatives like the Odisha Agriculture Drought Mitigation Programme with IRRI, and the Shree Anna Abhiyan-Odisha Millet Mission, the State government is taking steps to reduce paddy’s environmental footprint and encourage crop diversity.\n“An integrated intervention for alternative grains is crucial,” Dr. Chhatre said, adding that it “must include” extension and training services, involve self-help groups, and provide procurement support. “While encouraging sustainable paddy cultivation, policies must also prevent further expansion of paddy fields to curb emissions.”\nSharmila Vaidyanathan is an independent journalist from Bengaluru.\nPublished - July 23, 2026 09:15 am IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/science/india-irrigated-rice-fields-world-top-methane-sources/article71241002.ece", "date": "2026-07-23"}

{"title": "Possession with purpose unlocks Spain’s World Cup puzzle", "content": "The oldest footballing lesson in Spain has always been deceptively simple. If you have the ball, the opponent cannot score.\nFor years, however, that philosophy became both its greatest gift and its greatest burden. Spain monopolised possession, accumulated passes and controlled territory, but too often it left tournaments wondering whether beautiful football alone could still win the biggest prizes. The echoes of tiki-taka lingered long after the golden generation had faded, sometimes becoming an identity that imprisoned rather than liberated.\nAt this World Cup, Spain did not abandon its football. It rediscovered its purpose.\nLuis de la Fuente’s world champions finished the tournament with the best defence, conceding only one goal in eight matches. They dominated possession as La Roja always have, but possession was no longer the destination. It became the platform from which every other part of the game flourished. They pressed ferociously when they lost the ball, attacked vertically when spaces opened and defended with a discipline that suffocated some of the world’s finest forwards.\nBy the time Rodri lifted the trophy after the 1-0 victory over Argentina, Spain had beaten Portugal, Belgium, France and the defending champion in successive knockout rounds. There could be little argument about the legitimacy of its crown.\nThe numbers only reinforced what the eye had already seen. France had arrived in the semifinal with the tournament’s most feared attack. Kylian Mbappe, Ousmane Dembele and Michael Olise had combined for 13 goals and 10 assists in their first six matches. Spain reduced them to shadows. Mbappe failed to register a shot on target. France managed only three efforts on target all evening and generated barely 0.15 expected goals from its celebrated front three. Against Portugal, it accepted a tactical battle and found the goal required to make it past the Iberian neighbours. The Spain of Vicente del Bosque often appeared convinced that enough possession would eventually solve every problem. De la Fuente’s Spain understood that football offers many different questions.\nSometimes the answer was Lamine Yamal. Still only a teenager, Yamal entered the tournament carrying expectations that would have burdened far older footballers. His acceleration, disguised passing and fearlessness repeatedly tilted matches before opponents had organised themselves. Yet unlike so many young stars, he was never asked to carry Spain alone. Around him functioned a collective that was entirely free of hierarchy.\nRodri remained the team’s metronome, rarely hurried, forever choosing the correct pass before pressure arrived. Whenever Spain lost possession, the counter-press arrived almost instinctively, often recovering the ball before opponents could string together three passes.\nEvery attacker defended. Every defender initiated attacks. Possession, pressing and positional discipline became parts of the same movement rather than separate ideas.\nThere was also a maturity that distinguished this side from many previous champions.\nSpain rarely chased matches emotionally. It never seemed rushed by the occasion, whether facing Kylian Mbappe in Dallas, Belgium in Los Angeles or Lionel Messi in the MetLife Stadium. Its football carried the serenity of a team that knew exactly who it was.\nFor much of the past decade, international football has been shaped by transition, athleticism and chaos. Spain reminded everyone that control still matters. But it also demonstrated that control no longer means simply completing 800 passes.\nIt means controlling space, tempo, emotions and ultimately the result.\nIn doing so, de la Fuente’s players achieved something larger than lifting the World Cup. {"title": "Explained: What is the US-Saudi Arabia nuclear deal, and why is it raising concerns?", "content": "The United States and Saudi Arabia have announced a civil nuclear agreement that would allow the kingdom to develop a civilian nuclear energy programme with American technology. The deal, unveiled by the Trump Administration has also sparked criticism over the risks of nuclear proliferation and a possible arms race in the Middle East.\nThe agreement, known as a 123 Agreement under the US Atomic Energy Act, establishes a framework for civil nuclear cooperation between the two countries.\nUnder the pact:\n-Saudi Arabia will be able to develop a civilian nuclear energy programme with US technology.\n-American companies are expected to build nuclear reactors in the kingdom, generating contracts worth tens of billions of dollars over the coming decades.\n-The agreement supports Saudi Arabia's efforts to diversify its economy and reduce dependence on oil under its Vision 2030 programme.\n-The deal will now be submitted to the US Congress. Unless lawmakers reject it within the review period, it will come into force.\nThe Trump administration says the agreement complies with US non-proliferation laws and contains safeguards to ensure the programme remains peaceful.\nThis has become the biggest point of controversy.\nMultiple reports said the agreement would allow Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium and reprocess spent nuclear fuel—two activities that are essential for civilian nuclear power but can also provide the technological basis for producing nuclear weapons.\nHowever, President Donald Trump sought to clarify the issue on Truth Social, writing: \"There will be no enrichment of material!\"\nThe final text of the agreement has not yet been made public, leaving uncertainty over the exact enrichment provisions.\nThe agreement represents a major geopolitical victory for both Washington and Riyadh.\nFor the United States, it:\n-Strengthens ties with one of its closest Middle East allies.\n-Helps prevent Saudi Arabia from turning to China or Russia for nuclear technology.\n-Expands commercial opportunities for American nuclear companies.\nFor Saudi Arabia, it:\n-Advances its long-standing ambition to develop civilian nuclear energy.\n-Supports economic diversification beyond oil.\n-Gives Riyadh access to advanced US nuclear technology.\n1. Nuclear weapons risk\nCritics argue that uranium enrichment and spent-fuel reprocessing are technologies that can be used to produce weapons-grade material.\nAlthough enrichment for civilian reactors is typically low, the same infrastructure can theoretically be expanded for military purposes.\nSaudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has previously said that if Iran develops a nuclear weapon, Saudi Arabia would seek one as well.\n2. Weaker inspection requirements\nAnother major criticism is that the agreement reportedly does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency's Additional Protocol.\nThe Additional Protocol allows inspectors to conduct short-notice inspections at undeclared nuclear sites and is considered one of the strongest safeguards against secret nuclear activities.\nUnlike the Biden administration's earlier proposal, the Trump deal reportedly omits this requirement, raising concerns among non-proliferation experts.\n3. Risk of a regional arms race\nThe agreement comes while the United States is engaged in conflict with Iran over Tehran's nuclear programme.\nAnalysts warn that allowing Saudi Arabia greater nuclear capabilities could encourage other regional powers to pursue similar programmes, accelerating a Middle East nuclear competition.\n4. Congressional criticism\nSeveral US lawmakers have criticised the agreement.\nSenator Bernie Sanders argued that the deal contradicts Washington's stated objective of preventing nuclear proliferation, saying the administration is allowing Saudi Arabia to pursue capabilities similar to those it opposes in Iran.\nSenator Edward Markey warned the agreement \"would make us all less safe,\" arguing it could fuel an arms race in the region.\nThe Trump administration insists the agreement contains strong safeguards.\nSecretary of State Marco Rubio said any civil nuclear agreement would include protections to ensure it \"can't be turned into a weapons programme.\"\nEnergy Secretary Chris Wright described the pact as meeting \"the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation\" while strengthening US strategic and economic interests.\nYes—but there are conflicting signals.\nFor years, Washington sought to link any nuclear cooperation with Saudi Arabia to Riyadh normalising relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords.\nAfter the agreement was announced, Trump wrote on Truth Social that the deal would be approved only if Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham Accords.\nSaudi Arabia has repeatedly maintained that it will not recognise Israel without a credible pathway toward an independent Palestinian state.\n(With inputs from Reuters, AFP, AP)\nOops! {"title": "The ASEAN Championship: A regional tournament that became a cultural institution", "content": "A few days ago, Prime Minister Narendra Modi was in Jakarta speaking to the Indian community. He talked about the FIFA World Cup, joking that every time he visits Indonesia, football fever seems to be in the air.\nIndonesia is one of those places where football is discussed with the seriousness of politics and the emotion of a religion. While his reference was to highlight that he always visits Indonesia during a World Cup year, he was certainly briefed about the region’s passionate support for the game.\nThe final between Spain and Argentina has barely faded from television screens, while another tournament – the ASEAN Championship – is preparing to begin almost unnoticed outside the region. It is set to run from July 24 to August 26.\nThe ASEAN Championship is now thirty years old. When it began in 1996, it was a modest regional competition. Today it involves ten teams, and as many stadiums, across nine countries, a home-and-away group stage, and a level of fan engagement many larger football markets would envy.\nREAD | Spain refines its style, rekindles winning spree\nThe opening match this year will see Cambodia take on Singapore in Phnom Penh. If you had asked a football executive in Europe 20 years ago which country would host the largest stadium in an ASEAN tournament, Cambodia would not have been high on the list. And that has changed now, with Morodok Techo National Stadium capable of hosting 60,000 people – something that would’ve seemed improbable for Cambodian football a generation ago.\nStadiums are imperfect indicators of sporting success, but excellent indicators of political ambition. Governments rarely build large stadiums for ticket revenue; they build them to signal modernity, capacity, and relevance.\nI have always thought Southeast Asia is one of the world’s most underrated football regions. Not because the football is perfect – it isn’t – but because the relationship between football and society is unusually visible.\nTake the away fans. In Europe, travelling supporters are taken for granted. In ASEAN, they tell a different story. Millions of people move around the region for work. A Vietnamese worker in Singapore, a Cambodian worker in Thailand, an Indonesian family in Malaysia – these migration patterns create ready-made football communities. When Indonesia play away, they often find supporters already living in the host country. The tournament becomes less a series of international matches and more a map of Southeast Asian mobility.\nVietnam arrive as the defending champion and look like the region’s most coherent football project. Under Kim Sang-sik, the former South Korean World Cup player, Vietnam has done something unusual in Asian football: it has connected the senior team and the under-23 programme. The results have been almost suspiciously consistent: the 2024 ASEAN title, 2025 ASEAN under-23 success, 2026 SEA Games gold, and a third-place finish in the AFC under-23 championship. It feels less like a golden generation appearing by accident and more like an institution taking shape.\nThailand remains the old empire. It still carries the aura of the region’s historical power, much as Brazil does in South America even during less dominant periods. But empires rarely notice when the gap begins to close.\nREAD | Football is simple for complete midfielder Rodri\nIndonesia is the country that fascinates everyone in football. The population is enormous, the fan culture is volcanic, and the commercial upside is obvious. A recent goal celebration by former Oxford United youngster Marselino Ferdinan against Saudi Arabia went viral globally. That may sound trivial, but in modern football, a celebration becoming a meme is extremely valuable. It means the moment has escaped sport and entered culture.\nSingapore is the counterargument to population determinism. They recently qualified for the 2027 AFC Asian Cup ahead of much larger countries, including India and Bangladesh. Under Gavin Lee and Hariss Harun, Singapore has become a reminder that organisation can occasionally outperform demographics.\nThen there is the subject every federation discusses in corridors rather than at podiums: naturalisation.\nIndonesia, Vietnam, Cambodia, Singapore, and Malaysia have increasingly used foreign-born or naturalised players. In Southeast Asia, where dual citizenship is often unavailable for sporting purposes, players frequently have to give up their original nationality. That makes each decision more consequential than many observers realise.\nThe interesting question is not whether these players are “truly” national – football has always been shaped by migration – but whether the federation has built an environment compelling enough for someone to change their legal identity for it.\nMalaysia’s recent administrative crisis over naturalisation shows how quickly the issue can become political.\nHovering above the tournament is another curiosity: FIFA’s proposed ASEAN Cup later this year, with invited teams including India and, at least initially, China. The project remains hazy, but its existence raises a classic football question: what happens when a competition that grew organically suddenly finds itself sharing space with a globally branded version of itself?\nREAD | FIFA final: Spain’s absolute domination over Argentina explained\nThis is where the current ASEAN Championship becomes more interesting than its marketing suggests. For three decades it has grown because Southeast Asian audiences cared about it, not because anyone told them to or linked development funding to it. The colourful banners, packed away sections, loud anthems, and shirt-wearing commuters on match day were created by supporters before they were monetised by sponsors.\nIndian fans should probably pay attention. For years, they stayed awake at impossible hours to watch Europe. The ASEAN Championship offers something different: international football in a friendly time zone, free on YouTube, and taking place in countries that are geographically close but often absent from Indian football conversations.\nToday, when the first whistle blows in Phnom Penh, most of the global football industry will still be analysing Spain’s press against Argentina. Meanwhile, Southeast Asia will be doing what it has quietly done for thirty years: turning football into a regional language.\nAnd the rest of the world will eventually discover that the story was happening here all along.\n(The writer is the co-founder of SkaSports Investments Pvt Ltd and Director of two football clubs in Cambodia and Singapore)\nPublished - July 23, 2026 10:26 pm IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/sport/football/asean-championship-2026-southeast-asia-football-indonesia-vietnam-cambodia-singapore-malaysia-fifa-world-cup/article71259229.ece", "date": "2026-07-24"}

{"title": "Anti-paper leak law change moots stiffer penalty, wider coverage", "content": "New Delhi: Amid raging student protests over alleged examination irregularities, the government is set to strengthen its anti-paper leak law. Amendments to the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024, to be introduced in parliament on Monday, will propose hefty fines and bring state-level public examinations within its ambit, a senior government functionary said.\nThe proposed amendments, approved by the Union cabinet on Friday, come amid renewed concerns over examination integrity following the controversy surrounding the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET-UG) paper leak and mounting demands for stronger safeguards against organized examination fraud.\nAccording to the government functionary, the amendment Bill is expected to propose a fine of up to ₹10 crore for offences related to paper leaks and other organized examination malpractices, as against the existing maximum penalty of ₹1 crore for organized crimes under the law. The proposed reforms would also expand the scope of the law to cover all public examinations, including state-level.\nQuick answers to key questions\nThe proposed amendments to the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024, suggest hefty fines of up to ₹10 crore for offences related to paper leaks, significantly increasing the current maximum penalty of ₹1 crore.\nThe government aims to address renewed concerns over examination integrity following controversies such as the NEET-UG paper leak, amidst student protests demanding stricter safeguards against examination fraud.\nThe proposed amendment will broaden the scope of the law to include all public examinations conducted at the state level, in addition to those held by central agencies.\nThe Act covers a wide range of offences including leaking question papers, unauthorized access to exam materials, tampering with answer sheets, and conducting fake examinations for financial gain.\nLegal experts argue that institutional accountability must be strengthened alongside harsher penalties, advocating for statutory responsibilities on examination authorities and technology vendors to prevent leaks.\nAs the amendments are yet to be introduced in parliament, the final provisions will be known only after the Bill is tabled.\nThe move comes hours after Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in a late-night video message to protesting students on Thursday announced the government would introduce a Bill with stronger provisions against paper leaks during the ongoing Monsoon Session.\nThe Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024, which came into force on 21 June 2024, was brought in to curb paper leaks, organized cheating and other unfair practices in public examinations after widespread concerns over alleged irregularities in examinations such as NEET and UGC-NET. The legislation was introduced to create a dedicated legal framework to deal with offences committed by various entities involved in conducting public examinations by the central government and its agencies.\nThe law currently applies to examinations conducted by agencies including the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), Staff Selection Commission (SSC), Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs), Institute of Banking Personnel Selection (IBPS), National Testing Agency (NTA), and recruitment examinations held by central ministries and departments, besides other authorities notified by the Centre.\nEmails seeking comments from the cabinet secretariat, the ministries of education, higher education, and the Prime Minister's Office on Friday evening were not immediately answered.\nUnder the existing law, the offences are cognizable, non-bailable and non-compoundable. Individuals found guilty of using unfair means face imprisonment ranging from three to five years and a fine of up to ₹10 lakh, while service providers can be fined up to ₹1 crore, besides recovery of examination costs and debarment from conducting public examinations for four years. Organized examination fraud attracts imprisonment of five to ten years and a minimum fine of ₹1 crore, while properties of institutions involved may be attached and forfeited.\nThe law identifies a broad range of offences, including leaking question papers or answer keys, unauthorized access to question papers or OMR (optical mark recognition) sheets, tampering with answer sheets, manipulating seating arrangements, violating security protocols, hacking computer systems, creating fake examination websites, issuing fake admit cards and conducting fake examinations for monetary gain.\nThe move comes as paper leaks have emerged as a major political issue, with student protests over the NEET-UG examination spreading across the country. Opposition parties have demanded the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan and sought a discussion in Parliament over the examination irregularities.\nLegal experts said the proposed amendments reflect the changing nature of examination fraud but argued that institutional accountability must also be strengthened.\n\"The proposed amendments are significant because they acknowledge a hard truth—examination fraud is no longer a standalone offence but an organized criminal enterprise. Legally, paper leaks strike at the heart of Article 14 of the Constitution by denying similarly placed candidates an equal opportunity to compete,\" said Sonam Chandwani, managing partner at KS Legal & Associates.\nChandwani said the existing framework continues to focus predominantly on penal consequences after a leak has occurred. “The law must evolve to impose statutory accountability on examination authorities, technology vendors, and outsourced service providers entrusted with handling confidential material,” Chandwani said. \"If negligence or inadequate cybersecurity measures facilitate a leak, liability cannot be confined to the individuals found circulating question papers.\"\nThere is also a strong case for treating large-scale examination fraud on the same footing as other organized economic offences, with provisions for attachment of proceeds of crime, expedited trials, and mandatory blacklisting of entities involved, she said. \"A paper leak involving a national examination is not a victimless crime; it has identifiable victims running into lakhs of candidates. Ultimately, the credibility of the state is on trial every time a public examination is compromised. A law that only promises harsher punishment without ensuring institutional accountability will do little to restore public confidence,\" she added.\nSeparately, the Union cabinet on Friday approved two other proposals worth ₹4,294 crore. These include a ₹1,264-crore project for construction of the third and fourth railway lines on the 46-km Ballari-Guntakal section in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, and the Bhavya Rasayan Scheme with an outlay of ₹3,030 crore to set up three dedicated chemical parks across the country.\nThe railway proposal involves construction of the third and fourth railway lines on the 46-km Ballari-Guntakal section, spanning 24 km in Karnataka and 22 km in Andhra Pradesh. The additional railway lines will facilitate faster movement of freight from the Ballari-Hospete steel and cement clusters, improve connectivity to ports and enhance access to key tourist destinations.\nThe cabinet also approved the Bhavya Rasayan Scheme (Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojana-Rasayan), under which the Centre will provide financial assistance of up to ₹1,000 crore for each park, with states to be selected through a challenge-based competitive process. Each chemical park will have a minimum area of 8 square km and will be developed with plug-and-play infrastructure.\nHarsh Kumar is a policy reporter at Mint (HT Media Group), where he covers the Ministry of Commerce and Industry along with key departments of the Ministry of Finance, including the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA) and the Department of Financial Services (DFS). However, the Chief Justice-led Bench declined the request, with the Chief Justice telling the lawyer not to “waste” the court’s time. “We are not interested in videos. We don’t have time to watch them,” the CJI had said.\nAttempts to invoke the top court’s jurisdiction through letters date back to the late 1970s, when the court began relaxing the traditional rules of locus standi, allowing public-spirited individuals to approach the constitutional courts on behalf of aggrieved persons to protect fundamental rights and uphold the rule of law. This led to the evolution of the court’s epistolary jurisdiction, under which informal letters and postcards addressed to judges were treated as writ petitions with the objective of improving access to justice for the marginalised who had little or no meaningful access to the courts.\nOne of the earliest instances was Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration (1979), where the court treated a prisoner’s letter alleging custodial torture as a writ petition and issued directions to curb such practices.\nAgainst plainclothes personnel\nOne of the petitions before the top court seeks directions to regulate police action during public protests, including a prohibition on the deployment of plainclothes personnel for crowd-control duties, and guidelines governing the exercise of powers under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) that empowers a Executive Magistrate to act where “there is sufficient ground for proceeding under this section and immediate prevention or speedy remedy is desirable”.\n“The current generation of youth is experiencing deprivation, unemployment, expensive education, loneliness, and a sense of alienation and betrayal by their own government within their own country (violating Article 16). {"title": "The unfinished business of the India-U.K. trade deal | Explained", "content": "The story so far: The India-U.K. Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) came into force on July 15, 2026, cutting tariffs on 99% of Indian exports and loosening some mobility rules for professionals. But, as even Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal has said in the past, problematic issues have been left out of the deal, leaving the trade deal to include only those where there was agreement. There are three such key issues that remain unaddressed.\nWhy is investment missing from the deal?\nAlthough the title CETA includes the word ‘economic’, it is missing a dedicated section on investments, which does appear in other deals that India has negotiated, such as those with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) and New Zealand.\nThe deals with EFTA and New Zealand include a commitment from both parties to facilitate set amounts of investments into India. The U.K. agreement lacks this provision. One of the main reasons India and the U.K. have not been able to make headway on an investment treaty is the difference of opinion on how arbitration of disputes should be handled.\nIn 2017, India unilaterally cancelled nearly all the Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs) it had entered into, with the objective of reviewing them. An important provision of these BITs was that any dispute between a foreign investor and the Indian government would be arbitrated in a third country.\nThe cancellation of the BITs meant that foreign investors would have to first go through the full Indian legal process for a set period of time before availing of international arbitration, a prospect that has made several foreign investors balk.The India-U.K. BITs could not be completed along with the trade pact because of differences along these lines.\nWithout a BIT, investors have fewer treaty-based protections and no dedicated investor-state dispute mechanism if disputes arise.\nAlso Read | Maturing approach: On the India-U.K. Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement\nWhy won’t U.K. drugmakers gain wider access to India?\nEven though India has agreed to reduce tariffs, U.K. pharmaceutical companies will still find it difficult to gain wider access to the Indian market. During the negotiations, India held its position on Intellectual Property standards, resisting pressure to tweak its norms to enhance patent protection.\nIn particular, India fought to retain Section 3(d) of The Patents Act, 1970, which curbs the practice of “evergreening” by preventing pharma companies from obtaining fresh patents for minor modifications to a known drug unless they demonstrate enhanced therapeutic efficacy. Retaining this provision means that, if a modified version of the drug does not qualify for a new patent under Section 3(d), the original patent expires at the end of its term, allowing Indian pharmaceutical companies to manufacture generic versions of the drug, provided no other valid patents cover the product or its manufacture.\nAs a result, U.K. pharmaceutical exporters will continue to compete with Indian generic drug manufacturers in the Indian market. The data illustrates how this has played out in the past. The U.K. exports around £26 billion worth of medicines globally, but only £127 million, or 0.5%, goes to India. On the other hand, the U.K.’s National Health Service benefits significantly from access to low-cost Indian generic medicines manufactured in India.\nA U.K. Minister, giving evidence to a Parliamentary committee, acknowledged the limitation directly, saying he “would have liked to have been able to see us go further” on Intellectual Property, while noting that doing so would have required significant legislative change in India.\nWhy does the carbon tax remain an issue?\nThe U.K.’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), due to come into force from January 1, 2027, sits outside CETA entirely. It was not part of the CETA negotiations. Under CBAM, the U.K. will charge importers of carbon-intensive goods, such as steel, aluminium and cement, a fee roughly matching what a U.K. producer pays for the same emissions.\nIndian steel and aluminium exporters, whose production could be more carbon-intensive than that of U.K. producers, will have to bear the impact of the CBAM charge, even though they will receive lower import duties as a result of the CETA.\nThe U.K.’s trade commissioner for South Asia has stated the two were kept apart from the outset: “We made it clear from day one that CBAM was never part of the FTA”. Officials of the U.K. have said the issue will be addressed separately once it takes effect. For exporters, this means the tariff benefit they gain today could be offset by a carbon cost they face from 2027.\nThe saving grace is that the U.K. has not yet granted any country or regional bloc an exemption from the CBAM.\nWhat lies ahead?\nTaken together, these gaps point to a common pattern: CETA opens doors on tariffs and market access, but stops short of resolving the harder questions of legal protection, investment protection, and climate policy that sit around its edges. Professionals, investors, pharma exporters and carbon-intensive exporters will each be watching how, and whether, those gaps are addressed over time.\nPublished - July 24, 2026 11:32 pm IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/business/Economy/the-unfinished-business-of-the-india-uk-trade-deal-explained/article71256650.ece", "date": "2026-07-25"}

{"title": "Florida's first underwater habitat in 40 years will soon host scientists", "content": "A new underwater habitat has taken its place on the seabed off the Florida Keys, offering scientists something they have not had in US waters for decades: a permanent place to live and work beneath the ocean for days at a time. Ocean infrastructure company DEEP has installed its Vanguard pilot habitat at Tennessee Reef inside the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary. Positioned 17 metres (56 feet) below the surface, the structure is entering its final commissioning phase before hosting its first research crews. It is the first open-ocean subsea human habitat to be built, tested and deployed in the United States in around 40 years, marking a return to long-duration underwater research after a lengthy gap.\nHow DEEP installed the Vanguard underwater habitat in the Florida Keys\nThe deployment required a carefully planned offshore operation. Engineers first secured a foundation on the seabed before attaching the cylindrical habitat and connecting it to a nearby surface support buoy. The completed system now rests on a sandy section of the reef at a depth suitable for saturation-style missions. According to Ocean Science and Technology, the habitat's living section stretches 10.7 metres in length and around 2.5 metres in diameter.\n Once certification work is complete, it will be able to accommodate four aquanauts for research expeditions lasting at least five days.\nSea acceptance testing is currently underway ahead of classification by maritime assurance organisation DNV. DEEP will then begin training habitat support crews before the first operational missions commence. According to Ocean Science and Technology, Norman Smith, DEEP's Chief Technology Officer, the installation followed around 18 months of design, construction and testing.\n“Installing Vanguard at Tennessee Reef was a carefully choreographed marine operation with a lot of moving parts,\" Smith said, adding that successful deployment moves the company closer to enabling \"a continuous human presence in the ocean\" and expanding access for marine science, environmental monitoring and extreme-environment training.\nHow the Vanguard underwater habitat will study human health beneath the ocean\nAlthough coral reefs and marine ecosystems will be among Vanguard's primary research targets, the habitat has another role that receives less public attention: studying the people living inside it.\nReportedly, DEEP Director of Scientific Research, Dawn Kernagis, explained that underwater habitats create opportunities across three areas of science. Alongside marine research and testing life-support technologies, scientists can examine how the human body responds to prolonged exposure beneath the sea.\nAccording to Kernagis, underwater environments share several characteristics with other extreme settings such as spaceflight and high-altitude expeditions. \"You're potentially breathing different gases, you're at different pressure exposures, and you see changes in how the body functions, from the molecular level to the cardiovascular and nervous system,\" she wrote. Those physiological changes allow researchers to understand how healthy people respond to unusual environmental stress before applying those findings to medicine on land.\nHow the Vanguard underwater habitat could transform human health research\nScientists have investigated saturation divers for decades, but much of the available human research dates back many years. Advances in genetics, wearable monitoring, molecular biology and biomedical analysis now make it possible to observe biological responses with much greater precision than was previously achievable. As per reports, Kernagis said one of Vanguard's biggest advantages is that it functions as a laboratory rather than simply a place where divers sleep between missions.\nDuring earlier underwater projects, blood and tissue samples often had to be brought back to the surface before analysis. That introduced decompression-related changes, making it harder to separate the effects of living underwater from the effects of returning to normal atmospheric pressure. Processing biological samples while crews remain at depth could allow scientists to observe cellular and molecular responses in real time. She described that capability as potentially changing research across undersea medicine, immunology and human physiology.\nVanguard underwater habitat to advance coral research, medicine and astronaut training\nThe work planned for Vanguard extends well beyond studying divers themselves. The habitat will support coral restoration projects, continuous reef monitoring, climate impact assessments, species surveys, ocean sensor testing and astronaut training. Scientists also expect to use the platform for educational broadcasts, allowing audiences to communicate live with crews working on the seabed.\nHuman health research forms another part of that programme. Lessons from prolonged underwater missions could improve understanding of oxygen therapy, cardiovascular responses, immune function, sleep, nutrition, thermal regulation and continuous patient monitoring. Research into pressure exposure may also contribute to work involving hyperbaric medicine, wound healing and treatment for conditions such as carbon monoxide poisoning or gas embolism.\nFlorida Keys National Marine Sanctuary superintendent Eddie Kertis said subsea habitats have supported marine discoveries for decades and that the new installation creates additional opportunities for long-term scientific work while strengthening research infrastructure within the protected reef.", "link": "https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/world/us/florida-gets-its-first-underwater-research-habitat-in-around-40-years-where-scientists-will-soon-live-beneath-the-ocean/articleshow/132596443.cms", "date": "2026-07-25"}

Space is hard and such failures are not uncommon, but the almost steady clip of setbacks together with ISRO’s dispiritingly opaque public posture in the aftermath have raised concerns about systemic issues. In tandem, while the Indian space programme has introduced new commercial and policy initiatives, ISRO’s own launch frequency and scientific output have not increased.\nTo make matters worse, the Department of Space revealed in the second week of July that ISRO had received “a spate of requests” for resignation and voluntary retirement from Group-A scientific and technical personnel associated with Gaganyaan and other important missions. The Department added in a memo that such requests must no longer be accepted as a matter of routine.\nSupporting private enterprise\nContrary to some political rhetoric, start-ups will not substitute for ISRO’s increasingly noticeable failings. A strong private sector tends to emerge from a strong public ecosystem, rather than by displacing it. The foremost need is for the state to be the private sector’s anchor customer, a responsibility the state has thus far assumed to a remarkably minor degree.\nIndia also does not present enough domestic demand for satellite manufacturers and launch companies to subsist on. While venture capital’s appetite for Indian spaceflight is increasing, its interests are also better served by software-like growth trajectories. Launch vehicles and spacecraft manufacturing on the other hand need patient capital, present uncertain returns, and need rigorous regulatory oversight — which developmental finance is designed to absorb.\nMany start-ups initially recruit from ISRO, but when ISRO itself ceases to replenish its talent, both public and private sectors suffer. Indeed, it has become an institution consuming the technical knowledge it has accumulated over decades faster than it is being replenished. The government can no longer expect it to deliver increasingly ambitious technical outcomes while allowing the underlying stressors — including staffing, autonomy, transparency, pay, and technical leadership — to persist or even worsen.\nTacit knowledge\nIn the previous era, ISRO’s strength was rooted in its engineers’ power to say when a system was ready. But as it has become more politically salient, its major launches have become national events and political commitments in their own right and its engineering culture has become more pressure-driven, with unsurprising consequences for the psychological culture. Complex engineering organisations like ISRO depend on junior people feeling comfortable saying, “I think we are making a mistake.” But if they start to be concerned about how bad news will be received, they will simply elect to not escalate concerns.\nRocket science itself depends to a relatively great degree on tacit knowledge. A propulsion engineer may know ISRO adopted a particular weld specification after an obscure vibration issue 15 years ago, and such knowledge will not appear in the documentation. But accelerating retirements, delays in recruitment, and the departure of experienced people will also have eroded ISRO’s traditional culture of apprenticeship.\nFor as long as ISRO answered to Parliament, scientific and engineering peers, and the press, failure analysis reports and its researchers’ technical output were implicitly expected to withstand independent checks. While ISRO still answers to Parliament et al. on paper, accountability has flowed increasingly internal and increasingly vertical over the last decade, however, as failure analysis reports have been kept out of the public domain while its public communications have increasingly favoured promotional messaging over technical details.\nCart before horse\nNASA and Roscosmos both experienced versions of this change, as did Boeing’s commercial aircraft division. And as in those countries, the suffering is a symptom of a specific failure that is hard to diagnose in the here and now but which becomes obvious when the expected outcomes are confined to niches rather than becoming sustained.\nSpecifically, the country lacks mutually reinforcing institutions in the form of a technically excellent public agency, universities producing specialised talent, public research laboratories, reliable procurement, long-term financing, domestic customers presenting sufficient demand, and suppliers that can manage cyclical demand. In fact, India may have tried to liberalise the space economy before it built the industrial ecosystem that liberalisation presupposes.\nSans course correction, we must expect to have a weakening ISRO, a clutch of capable but relatively small private firms, continued dependence on the state (or even foreign suppliers) for the most advanced technologies, fewer scientists looking for long careers in the public sector, and a progressively fragmented ecosystem.\nExtractive state\nThe decline was not sudden and it was not inevitable. It has been sustained by a series of political and administrative choices that demanded more from ISRO without strengthening the institution itself. When the launch cadence had to increase, the engineering capacity did not. (Many launches slotted for 2026 are already delayed while NavIC is practically defunct.) When the strategic responsibilities multiplied, the workforce did not. When scientists resigned, the official memo restricted resignations instead of requiring authorities to discover and resolve the reasons they were leaving. When scientific or commercial missions failed, the transparency dropped. When the state pushed commercial activity, it did so without first ensuring the anchor institution was becoming stronger.\nA healthy state must protect its institutions from short-term pressures by giving them more money, autonomy, and legal authority, stable careers, and political cover when things go wrong. The Indian state did just this for much of ISRO’s history, but in the last decade or so, it has replaced its nurturing stewardship with a mandate that has treated, and still treats, ISRO as an asset to be mobilised. Rather than a productive state that continually enlarges the capacities of the institutions it governs, we have an extractive state that consumes those capacities to satisfy immediate fiscal, political, and strategic objectives.\nInstitutions do not sustain themselves. They need to be sustained or they will cannibalise themselves.\nmukunth.v@thehindu.co.in\nPublished - July 25, 2026 08:30 am IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/science/indian-state-draining-isro-hard-won-excellence/article71261853.ece", "date": "2026-07-25"}

{"title": "The Deschamps paradox: was his World Cup-winning Les Bleus tenure a success?", "content": "Dynasties rarely end with a bang. More often, they fade quietly, leaving only numbers and memories to tell the story.\nDidier Deschamps departs the France dugout after 187 matches in charge, having won 122 of them, drawn 32 and lost only 33 — a remarkable 65.2% win rate. But statistics alone cannot explain his tenure.\nRestoring credibility\nHe inherited a national team weighed down by embarrassment and disappointment when he succeeded Laurent Blanc in 2012. The side was still scarred by one of the darkest episodes in its footballing history. The disastrous 2010 World Cup campaign in South Africa had descended into chaos, culminating in the players’ infamous ‘mutiny’ against erstwhile manager Raymond Domenech. Blanc’s subsequent two-year spell did little to erase that stain.\nDeschamps’ first task was to restore France’s credibility. Fourteen years later, he walks away having delivered far more than most dared to expect, leaving behind a side that measures tournaments not by qualification, but by how far it goes.\nThe blueprint for Deschamps’ managerial philosophy was obvious to those who watched him play.\nALSO READ | Spain refines its style, rekindles winning spree with World Cup win\nFrom Nantes, Marseille and Juventus to the French national team, Deschamps captained almost every side he represented. Leadership came naturally, but so did another conviction that would shape his managerial career: an organised team will almost always outperform a collection of outstanding individuals. Yes, talent mattered. But the collective mattered more.\nAs a player, Deschamps made his name as a defensive midfielder whose greatest gifts were discipline, intelligence and relentless industry. His job was simple — recover possession and move the ball to those capable of creating something extraordinary. Eric Cantona’s famous nickname for him, ‘the water-carrier’, was less than complimentary. But it perfectly captured Deschamps’ willingness to sacrifice personal glory for the team’s success.\nThose same principles became the foundation of every French dressing room he commanded and helped him early on as he repaired a broken national side, both within the dressing room and beyond it.\nHis outfits mirrored him: relentless in their work rate, aggressive in their pressing, disciplined without the ball and exceptionally well organised. Superstars were encouraged, but never at the expense of team structure.\nThat pragmatism often made him an easy target for critics. What rarely received the same attention was his willingness to evolve. Over more than a decade in charge, Deschamps successfully navigated multiple generations of French talent — from Franck Ribery and Karim Benzema to Kylian Mbappe — adjusting his communication and leadership styles without ever compromising the standards he demanded.\nThe results speak for themselves. France reached the last four at the World Cup in three successive editions under Deschamps. It lifted the trophy in 2018, fell on penalties in the 2022 final and made a semifinal exit this year. In 2014, it was eliminated by eventual champion Germany in the quarterfinals. In England, a record like that would probably earn someone a knighthood — and then some.\n“I’m extremely happy. I’m very proud of everything we’ve done to reach this stage and to win a World Cup, to take the French team to the highest level,” Deschamps told the press at this year’s quadrennial showpiece.\nFinal-chapter irony\nThe irony is that his final chapter may have vindicated everything he had spent more than a decade preaching.\nFor years, Deschamps was criticised for being too cautious, too conservative, too reluctant to unleash France’s extraordinary attacking talent. In this World Cup, he defied his own patterns, loosened the reins and gave his star-studded side greater freedom. While that produced some of the tournament’s most attractive football, it would also be its undoing.\nWhen Spain ended its campaign, it was not because France lacked flair. It was because it was overrun. It cried out for the very qualities that had long defined Deschamps’ best teams: discipline, composure and control. If anything, it served as a reminder that putting the handbrake on is not always a sign of fear. Sometimes, it is simply what wins football matches, especially in knockout games at the highest level.\nUnlike many of football’s iconic players, Deschamps did not walk straight into elite managerial jobs on reputation alone. He earned his credentials by rebuilding clubs that needed rescuing. And he did it thrice.\nAS Monaco came first. Appointed in 2001, he guided it to second place in Ligue 1 in only his second season, finishing just one point behind title-winning Olympique Lyonnais. He followed it with the League Cup triumph, famous Champions League victories over Real Madrid and Chelsea, and a run all the way to the final before Jose Mourinho’s FC Porto proved too strong.\nThen came Juventus. Relegated to Serie B in the aftermath of the Calciopoli match-fixing scandal and burdened with a nine-point deduction, the Bianconeri needed stability as much as results. Deschamps delivered both, leading it straight back to Serie A as champion before resigning just a week after promotion following disagreements over transfer strategy.\nHis next revival came with Marseille, the club he had famously captained to Champions League glory as a player. In his first season, he ended an 18-year wait for the Ligue 1 title before adding three successive League Cups and two French Super Cups. Reawakening one of French football’s sleeping giants made him the obvious choice to succeed Blanc in 2012.\nALSO READ | Spain’s absolute domination over Argentina in the World Cup final explained\nHis record on the international stage is extraordinary. Five of the seven major tournaments in which France was eliminated under Deschamps ended with the team losing to the eventual champions. His tenure not only witnessed the makings of an enviable World Cup record, but also saw Les Bleus make the Euro final in 2016 and the semifinals in 2024.\nAnd yet, despite everything he achieved, one question will linger. Could he have accomplished even more?\nThat says as much about the extraordinary depth of French talent as it does about the man who guided it. Deschamps inherited a stable overflowing with gifted footballers, but his greatest achievement was moulding them into a side that consistently functioned as something greater than the sum of its parts.\nWhere the truth lies\nThe debate over his legacy will not disappear anytime soon. Critics will argue that his caution prevented France from reaching even greater heights. His supporters will counter that his discipline transformed limitless potential into sustained excellence. The truth, as is so often the case with the finest managerial careers, probably lies somewhere in between.\nPerhaps that is the paradox of Deschamps. The better France became under him, the more was expected of him. Winning the World Cup became the benchmark rather than the dream. Reaching the semifinals became routine instead of remarkable. All said and done, he leaves with France restored to where it belongs — among the game’s true heavyweights.\nAnother French legend, Zinedine Zidane, is widely tipped to be the man who follows him. Deschamps leaves behind a daunting assignment, though. His are far from impossible shoes to fill, but they are certainly not comfortable ones.\nPublished - July 25, 2026 01:55 am IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/sport/football/didier-deschamps-france-analysis-legacy-world-cup-zinedine-zidane-manager/article71263988.ece", "date": "2026-07-25"}

{"title": "Inside Ahmedabad's mega plan to host the 2030 CWG and 2036 Olympics", "content": "Ahmedabad’s appetite for bold bets can be measured in acres. At a recent planning summit, Indian Olympic Association (IOA) senior vice-president Ajay Patel offered a striking comparison. “Paris used 400 acres for its 2024 Games. Ahmedabad has already acquired 1,000 acres.”\nOfficially, the city is preparing for the 2030 Commonwealth Games (CWG), the centenary edition of the event and India’s first since Delhi 2010. But nearly every major decision being taken today is being shaped by a larger ambition: positioning Ahmedabad as the host city for the 2036 Olympic Games. “The 2030 CWG is a dress rehearsal for the 2036 Summer Olympic Games,” Patel said. While the International Olympic Committee (IOC) is expected to take a final call on the 2036 host around 2029, Gujarat has already begun building as though the Olympics are coming.\nA drive through Motera reflects the scale of that ambition. Construction cranes, excavators and scaffolding dominate the skyline as roads, sporting venues, transport systems and hotels take shape for an event still four years away.\nThe master plan\nAt the heart of the transformation is the Rs 5,050-crore \nSardar Vallabhbhai Patel Sports Enclave (SVPSE), coming up around the Narendra Modi Stadium, the world’s largest cricket venue with a capacity of 1.32 lakh. \nThe stadium is set to host the opening and closing ceremonies of the CWG. The enclave will include a 12,000-seat aquatics centre, an 18,000-seat tennis centre and indoor arenas for basketball, gymnastics, volleyball, skateboarding, artistic swimming and sport climbing. To make way for the project, the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC) altered land-use plans across Sabarmati and Koteshwar, freeing nearly 14.5 lakh square metres.\nUnlike several past multisport events where venues struggled to find a purpose after the Games, Gujarat says legacy planning has been built into the project from the outset. “We are adopting an asset utilisation model rather than a traditional ROI-based recovery approach,” Gujarat deputy chief minister Harsh Sanghavi, who led Ahmedabad’s CWG bid, told TOI . “The CWG infrastructure is a long-term investment in Ahmedabad’s transformation into an Olympic-ready global hub, not a sunk cost.” The venues will function as a year-round Games Plaza, hosting sporting events, concerts and exhibitions, with operational breakeven projected within five to seven years. A dedicated Infrastructure Legacy & Operations Trust (ILOT) is being created to manage the facilities at Motera and the Naranpura Sports Complex.\nThe sporting footprint extends well beyond Motera. Around 11km away, at Karai in Gandhinagar, a net-zero athletics stadium with a capacity of 50,000 and a worldclass shooting centre are under construction. The Rs 825-crore Naranpura Sports Complex is already operational, with facilities for badminton, squash, table tennis and Olympic-standard swimming.\nAdditional sports complexes have been completed in Vastral, while more are under construction in Gota, Ghuma, Naroda and Nikol. In all, 22 competition venues have been finalised across Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar. Sanghavi has set a firm deadline. “All major infrastructure will be ready by the end of 2029, leaving early 2030 for trial runs. By the time athletes and visitors arrive, Ahmedabad will be fully ready, with venues, transport and support systems functioning seamlessly.”\nThe 30-minute city\nThe makeover, however, extends far beyond stadiums. Ahmedabad’s vehicle population is growing by nearly nine per cent annually, significantly above the national average. To prevent congestion during the Games, planners have adopted what officials describe as a “30-minute city” model. The objective is simple: every athlete, official and spectator should be able to travel between venues, hotels and training centres within 30 minutes.\nThe existing 168km Bus Rapid Transit System (BRTS), which carries more than 2.2 lakh passengers a day, will be integrated with an expanding Metro network. A new northsouth Metro corridor and a parallel Neo Metro or light-rail system are each designed to carry around 70,000 passengers per hour in either direction.\nA Rs 472-crore integrated ticketing platform will allow commuters to use a single QR code across the Metro, BRTS and a planned fleet of 3,000 electric buses. The road network is also being expanded. New arterial roads and northsouth and east-west corridors are being developed, while more than 100 roads are being widened. At the same time, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Airport is preparing for a sharp rise in traffic. A new integrated terminal is expected to double its annual capacity, while airports at Dholera, Vadodara and Surat could help handle the overflow during the Olympics.\nBudgets and backers\nFinancing a project of this scale will require multiple funding streams. According to Gujarat’s Olympic bid estimates, the organising committee budget could range from Rs 18,557 crore to Rs 41,031 crore, while capital expenditure on infrastructure is projected at between Rs 16,060 crore and Rs 22,878 crore. The state plans to rely heavily on public-private partnerships, particularly for the Olympic Village and International Broadcast Centre. It is also proposing an ‘Adopt a Sport’ programme to encourage corporations to support athlete development and infrastructure through corporate social responsibility funding.\nOfficials cite Gujarat’s own sporting investment as evidence of its long-term commitment. The state’s sports budget has risen from Rs 2.5 crore in 2002 to Rs 521 crore today, while the Khel Mahakumbh programme now attracts more than seven million participants annually.\nVillage and vacancy\nAccommodation remains one of the biggest challenges. The proposed Olympic Village, located within 5km of the Narendra Modi Stadium, will comprise 2,191 apartments capable of housing more than 17,500 athletes. The apartments are intended to be converted into premium residential housing.\nThe shortage of hotels presents an even tougher problem. Ahmedabad currently has just over 5,400 star-category rooms, while the long-term requirement for an Olympics is estimated at close to one lakh. The target is to increase capacity to 40,000 rooms before the 2030 Commonwealth Games through a new hotel policy offering capital subsidies. Parcels of land have already been earmarked for development, while neighbouring cities such as Vadodara and Mehsana are expected to absorb some of the additional demand.\nGreen promises\nThe transformation also carries an ambitious sustainability agenda. Ahmedabad has committed to powering the proposed Olympics Games entirely through renewable energy, backed by upgraded battery-storage systems. Six million trees have already been planted against a target of 10 million, while every competition venue is expected to recycle and reuse all wastewater.\n(With inputs from Kapil Dave and Parag Dave)", "link": "https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/sports/more-sports/others/the-great-games-gambit-inside-ahmedabads-mega-plan-to-host-the-2030-cwg-and-2036-olympics/articleshow/132618235.cms", "date": "2026-07-25"}

{"title": "RBI, govt measures could turn India's balance of payments surplus, ease pressure on rupee: HDFC", "content": "New Delhi [India]: India's balance of payments (BoP) could return to a small surplus instead of recording a third consecutive annual deficit following a series of measures announced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the government in June, according to HDFC Mutual Fund's July report.\nThe report said the measures could ease pressure on the rupee by improving capital inflows and strengthening the country's external position.\n\"The RBI and government's June measures could turn what could have been a third straight year of balance-of-payments deficit into a small surplus, thereby taking pressure off the rupee,\" the report said.\nAccording to the report, the RBI's decision to bear the full hedging cost for fresh three-to-five-year FCNR(B) deposits until September 30, 2026, could attract potential inflows of USD 40-60 billion. It added that around USD 17 billion had already been mobilised under this route as of July 17, 2026.\nThe report also said the concessional foreign exchange swap facility for external commercial borrowings by public sector undertakings could attract another USD 15-25 billion in inflows while reducing hedging costs. It added that the expansion of the Fully Accessible Route (FAR) for government securities and the removal of foreign portfolio investment limits on short-term investments would improve the flexibility and accessibility of investments in Indian government bonds.\nFurther, the report noted that the government's decision to withdraw capital gains and withholding tax on returns from investments in government securities increases the likelihood of Indian bonds being included in the Bloomberg bond index at its next review. Such inclusion could potentially attract USD 10-20 billion over the next 12-18 months, it added.\nThe report said the depreciation of the rupee over the past 12-18 months has been driven largely by weaker capital flows rather than weak economic fundamentals. {"title": "Early trends show women make two-third of revamped rural job scheme workforce", "content": "New Delhi: India's revamped rural jobs programme is emerging as an early driver of women's economic participation, with them contributing nearly two-thirds of the work generated in the scheme's first three weeks, according to government officials and data reviewed by Mint. The development can be attributed to the scheme's expanded and more inclusive framework, which has opened up new avenues beyond manual labour, the officials said.\nWomen accounted for over 63% of the 4.62 crore person-days generated under the Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-GRAM G) during 1-20 July, the first 20 days of rollout. A ‘person-day’ here means one person employed for one day. So, if 100 workers are employed for 10 days each, it generates 1,000 person-days of employment under the scheme.\nThe data for women's participation in July 2025 under the erstwhile Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) is not available. In the entire financial year 2026, women accounted for 57.3% of the total person-days, the data showed.\nFor context, in July 2025, MGNREGA had generated 201.78 lakh person-days of employment, and this year, it generated 174.35 in April, 274.01 lakh in May and 292.95 lakh in June before the revamped scheme was adopted.\nAccording to the data, the states where women's participation has exceeded the national average include Kerala (participation was 89%), Tamil Nadu (87%), Rajasthan (74%), Himachal Pradesh (70%), Assam (67%), Manipur (65%) and Andhra Pradesh (64%).\nUnder the revamped scheme, women are taking up leadership roles, with around 61% worksites appointing them as supervisors (or mates) for strengthening workplace monitoring and community engagement.\nThe expanded work framework includes roles such as worksite supervisors, participation in social audits and employment in managing nurseries, compost and vermi-compost units, self-help group (SHG) infrastructure, storage facilities and rural haats, among others.\nIn response to an email query, Rohit Kansal, secretary in the rural development ministry said, \"With women contributing over 63% of the total person days generated so far and assuming leadership roles as ‘mates’ at a large number of worksites, VB GRAM G is emerging as a strong platform for women's economic empowerment and grassroots leadership.\"\n\"This momentum is being reinforced through policy measures that address the practical barriers to women's participation. The VB GRAM G Act incorporates a dedicated childcare provision, under which a woman worker is appointed and paid at the prescribed wage rate at worksites where five or more children below the age of five are present,\" he added.\nBy integrating childcare and support with employment, the framework seeks to make rural public works more inclusive, gender-responsive and conducive to sustained participation of women in the workforce.\nUnder the VB-GRAM G scheme, the statutory employment guarantee has been expanded to 125 days from 100 days under MGNREGA. Under MGNREGA, the Central government bore 100% of the wage costs, or bulk of the expenditure, and states contributed 25% of the material costs. However, under the new norms, the Centre will fund only 60% of the total cost in most states, and 90% in north-eastern and Himalayan states; with states funding the balance.\nThe national average notified daily wage has been raised from ₹298.8 under the erstwhile MGNREGA to ₹327.4 under VB–G RAM G, representing an average increase of ₹28.6 per day. The minimum notified wage under the scheme is ₹300 per day.\nEarly trends suggest the programme is evolving beyond a wage-employment scheme into a community-led initiative that promotes women's economic empowerment and participation in rural governance, the officials said.\nThe government officials cited above said women supervisors are playing a key role in digital governance by using face-authentication systems to record attendance and manage e-KYC, helping improve beneficiary identification, transparency and accountability.\nThe rural job plan also has other welfare benefits: every worksite must provide clean drinking water, shaded rest areas and first-aid kits. The law also guarantees free medical treatment for workers injured on duty, including hospitalization, medicines, accommodation and a daily allowance equal to half the wage rate. In cases of death or permanent disability, ex gratia compensation will be provided under the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana.\nThe law also provides a legal guarantee for worksite facilities, ensuring dignity, safety and social security for all workers, including women. These measures are aimed at creating a safer and more supportive working environment, which has resulted in higher participation, the officials said.\nVB-GRAM G, notified earlier this year, marks the government's attempt to recast India's rural employment architecture by combining wage employment with livelihood creation, rural infrastructure development and asset generation.\nThe scheme strengthens transparency through mandatory Janata Boards displaying project details, weekly public disclosures, geo-tagging of assets, real-time monitoring dashboards, mobile-based inspections and enhanced social audits. These measures aim to improve public oversight and accountability in rural employment work implementation.\nNow, for durable outcomes\nExperts say the encouraging early trends on women's participation must now be backed by consistent implementation to ensure the scheme delivers durable livelihoods rather than short-term employment.\n“The early numbers are promising and reflect the growing willingness of rural women to participate in the workforce when employment opportunities are backed by better wages and supportive worksite conditions. But participation alone should not be the benchmark for success,” said Ashish Kumar Singh, president of Citizen Forum, a civil rights group in Bihar.\n“The scheme's long-term impact will depend on whether it improves household incomes, creates productive community assets and delivers timely wages with adequate transparency,\" Singh said.\n\"The early trend suggests that the scheme is creating opportunities for women beyond traditional wage labour. If the initial trends continue and are supported by timely payments and quality implementation, VB–GRAM G could become an important instrument for strengthening women's economic participation in rural India,\" said Rakesh Arrawatia, professor at the Institute of Rural Management Anand (IRMA) and dean at School of Cooperative Banking and Finance.\nThe Centre has allocated ₹95,692.31 crore for the VB-G RAM G scheme in FY27, up from the record ₹86,000 crore provided for MGNREGA in FY25, a level retained in the FY26 budget.\nThe early employment trends in the rural job scheme come against the backdrop of rural households reporting the weakest income momentum since state-run National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (Nabard) began tracking economic conditions nearly two years ago.
