{"title": "Foreign Assets Disclosure Scheme 2026: ₹1 crore limit, 30% tax and December 31 deadline — all you need to know", "content": "The scheme, notified under the Finance Act, 2026, will remain open until December 31, 2026, and covers foreign assets and income subject to specified monetary limits. Under the scheme, taxpayers can disclose undisclosed foreign assets or income of up to ₹1 crore, while certain foreign assets that were already offered to tax but not reported in the relevant return schedule can be declared if their aggregate value does not exceed ₹5 crore.\nThe FAQs detail who can use the scheme, what can be declared, how foreign assets will be valued, the filing and payment process, and the benefits and exclusions under the scheme.\nThe Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (Chapter IV, sections 130 to 144 of th\nFinance Act, 2026, read with the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers – Disclosure Scheme Rules, 2026)\nA. About the Scheme\nQ1. What is the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers - Disclosure Scheme, 2026?\nAns: It is a one-time voluntary disclosure scheme contained in Chapter IV (sections 130 to 144) of the\nFinance Act, 2026. It enables eligible taxpayers to declare certain undisclosed foreign assets, undisclosed\nforeign income, or undeclared foreign assets, on payment of a specified tax or fee.\nQ2. What does the Scheme commence?\nAns: The Scheme comes into force on 16th August, 2026.\nQ3. What is the “last date” for filing a declaration?\nAns: The last date has been fixed as 31st December, 2026. No declaration can be filed after this date.\nQ4. What is the “valuation date” for the Scheme?\nAns: The valuation date is 31st March, 2026. The fair market value of assets proposed to be declared\nmust be computed as on this date.\nQ5. Which income-tax authority administers declarations under the Scheme?\nAns: The “income-tax authority” for the purposes of the Scheme is the Principal Director General of\nIncome-tax (Systems) or the Director General of Income-tax (Systems), as the case may be. The entire\nprocess will be done online.\nB. Who Can Make a Declaration (Eligibility)\nQ6. Who is the “assessee” eligible to declare under the Scheme?\nAns: An “assessee” eligible under the scheme is one —\n(i) who is resident in India, (as per section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 1961), in the relevant previous\nyear; or\n(ii) who is a non-resident, or resident but not ordinarily resident (RNOR), [as per section 6(6) of\nthe Income-tax Act, 1961], in the relevant previous year, but was resident in India either-\n(A) in the previous year to which the undisclosed foreign income under section 4 of the\nBlack Money Act, 2015 relates, or\n(B) in the previous year in which the undisclosed asset located outside India was acquired.\nAlso Read: Taxation laws (Amendment) Bill to attract more foreign capital, provide policy certainty introduced in LS\nQ7. Can a person who is presently a non-resident still make a declaration?\nAns: Yes, a person being a non-resident but was resident in India either\n(i)in the year to which the undisclosed income relates; or\n(ii)in the year in which the undisclosed asset was acquired\ncan make a declaration.\n1FAST-DS: FAQs\nQ8. Is RNOR (Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident) status relevant?\nAns: Yes. The definition of “assessee” specifically covers non-resident and RNOR persons who meet the\nresidency conditions noted above. The declarant can state his residential status for the previous year of\nacquisition of the asset or earning of the income in Form 1.\nQ9. On what grounds can a declaration be made?\nAns: A declaration may be made where the assessee —\n(a) has failed to furnish a return under section 139 of the Income-tax Act, 1961; or\n(b) has failed to disclose the asset or income in a return furnished before the Scheme\ncommenced; or\n(c) such asset or income has escaped assessment within the meaning of section 147 of the\nIncome-tax Act, 1961.\nQ10. Within what time-window must the declaration be filed?\nAns: On or after the date of commencement of the Scheme, but on or before the last date (i.e., between\n16th August 2026 and 31st December, 2026).\nQ11. Can a declaration be made for any previous year?\nAns: Yes, a declaration can be made for any previous year in respect of income or assets covered by the\nTable in section 133, subject to the monetary thresholds and other conditions of the Scheme.\nC. What Can Be Declared — Scope of the declaration\nQ12. What are the categories of declaration recognised under the Scheme?\nAns: There are two broad categories of declaration —\na) an undisclosed asset located outside India or undisclosed foreign income which was not\noffered to tax. [Section 133 – Table: Sl. No. 1]\nb) an asset located outside India, which was already offered to tax or was acquired when the\nassessee was a non-resident, but not declared in the relevant Schedule of the return. [Section\n133 – Table: Sl. No. 2]\nQ13. What does “undisclosed asset located outside India” mean?\nAns: An asset (including a financial interest in any entity) located outside India, held by the assessee in\nhis own name or in respect of which he is the beneficial owner, where he has no explanation about the\nsource of investment, or the explanation given is, in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, unsatisfactory.\nQ14. What does “undisclosed foreign income” mean?\nAns: The total amount of income of an assessee from a source located outside India, which was\nchargeable to tax in India but which has not been offered to tax.\nQ15. What is the monetary threshold for a declaration under Section 133 – (Table: Sl. No. 1)?\nAns: The aggregate value of the undisclosed asset located outside India (as on 31st March, 2026) and\nthe undisclosed foreign income must not exceed ₹1 crore.\n2FAST-DS: FAQs\nQ16. What is the monetary threshold for a declaration under Section 133 – (Table: Sl. No. 2)?\nAns: The aggregate value of the assets located outside India must not exceed ₹5 crore.\nD. Amount Payable\nQ17. What is the amount payable for a declaration under Section 133 – (Table: Sl. No. 1)?\nAns: The total amount payable would be the aggregate of -\n(i)tax of 30% of the value of the undisclosed asset located outside India or 30% of the\nundisclosed foreign income declared; and\n(ii)amount equal to the tax paid in (i)\nQ18. Please explain this with an example?\nAns: Where an undisclosed foreign bank account is valued at ₹60 lakh and undisclosed foreign income\nis ₹20 lakh, the aggregate payable is Rs 48 Lakh as given below\nSi.No Description Value/Income Tax payable Additional 100%\nTOTAL Amount\nof tax payable\npayable\n1 Foreign bank account 60 Lakh 18 Lakh 18 Lakh 36 Lakh\n2 Foreign income 20 Lakh 6 Lakh 6 Lakh 12 Lakh\nTOTAL 24 Lakh 24 Lakh 48 Lakh\nQ19. What is the amount payable for a declaration under Section 133 – (Table: Sl. No. 2)?\nAns: A flat fee of ₹1 lakh, provided the aggregate value of the assets located outside India does not\nexceed ₹5 crore.\nQ.20 What is the amount payable if the aggregate value of the assets located outside India is Rs 6.5\nCr?\nAns: If the value of the assets is more than Rs 5 Cr, the assessee will not be eligible to avail the scheme.\nE. Valuation of Assets (Rule 3)\nQ21. What is the general approach for computing fair market value (FMV)?\nAns: As a general rule, FMV is the higher of\n(a) the cost of acquisition, and\n(b) the price the asset would ordinarily fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation date,\nideally supported by a report from a valuer recognised by the government (or its agency) of\nthe country where the asset is located.\nWhere such market valuation is not carried out, the indexed cost of acquisition is deemed to be the fair\nmarket value.\n3FAST-DS: FAQs\nQ22. How is FMV computed for bullion, jewellery or precious stones?\nAns: FMV is the higher of the cost of acquisition and its open-market price on the valuation date\n(supported by a recognised valuer’s report); if such valuation is not carried out, the indexed cost of\nacquisition shall be the FMV.\nQ23. How is FMV computed for archaeological collections, paintings, sculptures or other artistic\nworks?\nAns: FMV is the higher of the cost of acquisition and its open-market price on the valuation date\n(supported by a recognised valuer’s report); if such valuation is not carried out, the indexed cost of\nacquisition shall be the FMV.\nQ24. How is FMV computed for quoted shares and securities?\nAns: FMV is the higher of the cost of acquisition and the average of the lowest and highest price quoted\non an established securities market on the valuation date;\nQ.25 In case there is no trading of quoted shares and securities on the valuation date, how is the FMV\ncalculated?\nAns: In case of no trading on valuation date, the FMV is the average of the lowest and highest price on\nthe nearest preceding date on which the shares/securities were traded.\nQ26. How is FMV computed for unquoted equity shares?\nAns: FMV is the higher of the cost of acquisition and the value computed by a prescribed formula based\non the book value of specified assets, the fair market value of bullion, jewellery, shares, securities and\nimmovable property, liabilities (excluding specified items such as paid-up capital and reserves), and the\npaid-up value of the equity shares. If this valuation is not carried out, indexed cost of acquisition is\ndeemed to be the FMV.\nQ27. How is FMV computed for unquoted shares/securities other than equity shares?\nAns: FMV is the higher of cost of acquisition and the open-market price (the price that the share or\nsecurities would ordinarily fetch if sold on the open market) on the valuation date, supported by a\nrecognised valuer’s report; if such valuation is not carried out, the indexed cost of acquisition shall be\nthe FMV.\nQ28. How is FMV computed for immovable property located outside India?\nAns: FMV is the higher of the cost of acquisition and the open-market price on the valuation date, as per\na valuation report from a valuer recognised by the government (or its agency) of the country where the\nproperty is located; if such valuation is not carried out, the indexed cost of acquisition shall be the FMV.\nQ29. How is FMV computed for a foreign bank account?\nAns: The value shall be the sum of all deposits made into the account from the date it was opened up to\nthe valuation date. However, certain exclusions are allowed.\n where the account (or a part of it) was earlier declared under Chapter VI of the Black Money Act,\n2015, and tax and penalty were charged on the value so computed, only deposits made since the\ndate of that earlier declaration are aggregated.4FAST-DS: FAQs\n deposits made out of the proceeds of a withdrawal from the same account are also excluded, to\navoid double counting.\nQ30. Please explain this with an example.\nAns: Yes. An assessee had opened a foreign bank account (BA) in 2010. The following deposits and\nwithdrawals were made in BA since then. Assuming that the withdrawals made were late re-deposited\ninto the BA, the value of the asset shall be calculated as follows.\nDate Deposits Withdrawals Calculation of\nvalue of asset\n01.04.2010 $ 1,000 - $ 1,000\n01.06.2011 $ 500 - $ 500\n01.08.2011 - $ 700 -\n01.04.2012 $ 500 - -\n01.08.2013 $ 500 - $ 300\n01.04.2019 $2,500 - $ 2,500\n01.06.2020 - $ 400 -\n01.09.2021 $ 1,000 - $ 600\n01.05.2024 - $ 500 -\nTOTAL $ 4,900\nThe value of this asset i.e $ 4,900 will be converted into Rupees as on 31.03.2026 for the purpose of\nvaluation under these Rules.\nQ31. Please explain this with an example if the account was already declared under Chapter VI of the\nBlack Money Act, 2015.\nAns: If the above taxpayer in Q.30 had declared the deposits made in the above account under Chapter\nVI of the Black Money Act, 2015, the value of the asset shall be the sum of the deposits made since such\ndate. In that case, the value of the asset shall be calculated as follows, assuming that the withdrawals\nmade were late re-deposited into the BA.\nDate Deposits Withdrawals Calculation of\nvalue of asset\n01.04.2019 $2,500 - $ 2,500\n01.06.2020 - $ 400 -\n01.09.2021 $ 1,000 - $ 600\n01.05.2024 - $ 500 -\nTOTAL $ 3,100\nThe value of this asset i.e $ 3,100 will be converted into Rupees as on 31.03.2026 for the purpose of\nvaluation under these Rules.\nQ32. How is FMV computed for an interest in a foreign partnership firm, association of persons, or\nLLP?\nAns: The value of an interest is calculated in the following steps\n5FAST-DS: FAQs\n The net assets of the firm/AOP/LLP are first determined as on the valuation date.\n The portion of net assets equal to the capital contributed is allocated among partners/members\nin the ratio of capital contribution;\n The residual net assets are allocated as per the partnership/association agreement for\ndistribution on dissolution, or, in its absence, in the profit-sharing ratio.\nQ33. How is FMV computed for residuary assets (where an explicit valuation method is not provided)?\nAns: FMV is the higher of its cost of acquisition/amount invested and the price it would fetch if sold in\nthe open market on the valuation date in an arm’s-length transaction; if such valuation is not carried\nout, the indexed cost of acquisition shall be the FMV.\nQ34. What if sale proceeds of one asset, or a withdrawal from a bank account, were used to acquire\nanother asset?\nAns: To prevent the same value being counted twice, the FMV of the old asset (or the bank account, as\nthe case may be) is reduced by the amount reinvested in the new asset.\nFor example, where a house property was sold and the proceeds deposited in a bank account, and part\nof that account was later used to buy another property, the FMV of the bank account is reduced by the\namount invested in the new property, while the new property is separately valued at its own FMV.\nQ35. In what currency is value to be reported, and how is foreign currency converted?\nAns: All values are to be reported in Indian Rupees. For conversion of foreign currency:-\n Where the currency in which the value is expressed is one of the currencies designated by the\nReserve Bank of India under the Foreign Exchange Management (Deposit) Regulations, 2016, it\nis converted into Indian Rupees at the RBI’s reference rate on the valuation date.\n If it is not such a designated currency, it is first converted into US Dollars at the rate specified by\nthe central bank (or, failing that, another regulated bank) of the country where the asset is\nlocated, and the US Dollar value is then converted into Indian Rupees at the RBI reference rate\non the valuation date.\nQ36. Further, the income or amount of\ninvestment in the asset declared under this scheme shall not be included in the total income of the\ntaxpayer under the Income-tax Act, 1961 or the Black Money Act, 2015.\nQ49. Further, the income or amount of investment in the asset declared under this scheme shall not be included in the total income of the taxpayer under the Income-tax Act, 1961 or the Black Money Act, 2015, the department said.\nPublished on August 15, 2026", "link": "https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/economy/income-tax-department-rolls-out-foreign-asset-disclosure-scheme-for-small-taxpayers/article71348642.ece", "date": "2026-08-16"}

{"title": "Quote of the day by Plato: \"The heaviest penalty for declining to rule is…\"", "content": "Leadership can look appealing from a distance, but taking responsibility for other people’s decisions, work or wellbeing is rarely as simple as holding a title. There are times when people step forward because they want authority, and others when they do so because nobody else is willing to take responsibility. Plato’s famous observation examines the other side of that choice. “The heaviest penalty for declining to rule is to be ruled by someone inferior to yourself”. The thought is not simply an argument for seeking power. It raises a more difficult question about what happens when people who may be capable of making sound decisions choose not to participate. For Plato, avoiding responsibility could carry its own cost. The quote of the day offers a way to think about leadership, judgement, competence and the consequences of leaving important decisions to others.\nQuote of the day by Plato\n“The heaviest penalty for declining to rule is to be ruled by someone inferior to yourself.”\nWhat Plato’s words actually mean\nPlato was interested in the responsibilities attached to governing and in the qualities that make someone suitable to hold authority. His observation suggests that refusing to take responsibility does not mean removing yourself from the consequences of decisions. Someone else will still make them.\nImagine a workplace where an experienced employee repeatedly avoids taking a leadership role because they do not want the additional pressure. \nA less experienced person eventually takes charge and makes decisions that the first employee considers poor. The experienced employee may have avoided the stress of leadership, but they have not avoided its consequences.\nThe same principle can apply to smaller situations. A group has to choose between several options. Someone with useful knowledge stays quiet because they do not want an argument. The decision goes another way. Later, they realise that their input might have changed the outcome.\nPlato’s point is not that stepping forward is always right. It is that stepping back is not always neutral.\nPlato’s journey from Athens to one of philosophy’s most influential ideas\nPlato was born around 427 BC in Athens or its surrounding area and came from a wealthy family. He became closely associated with Socrates, whose questioning method had a major influence on his philosophical thinking.\nThe death of Socrates in 399 BC was an important event in Plato’s life. Socrates was convicted by an Athenian jury and sentenced to death, an episode that contributed to Plato’s concerns about justice, political decision-making and the reliability of public judgement.\nPlato later founded the Academy in Athens, where philosophy and other areas of learning were studied. Aristotle was among those who studied there. Much of Plato’s work was written in the form of dialogues, allowing different characters to question assumptions and examine competing ideas. The Republic, where the quotation is found, deals with justice, education, politics and the organisation of society.\nHis political ideas were far removed from the structure of modern democracies. Yet his questions about who should govern and what qualifies someone to exercise authority have remained subjects of discussion for centuries.Why refusing responsibility can have consequences\nPeople often have good reasons for avoiding leadership. A senior position can mean longer hours, difficult decisions, disagreements with colleagues and greater accountability when something goes wrong. Remaining outside the decision-making process can seem like the easier option.\nBut decisions still have to be made. A project needs somebody to decide its direction. A team needs priorities. A community needs people willing to organise its affairs. A company needs people who can make choices when there is no obvious answer.\nIf capable people consistently refuse those responsibilities, somebody else eventually takes them on.\nThat person may turn out to be perfectly capable. Plato’s argument does not guarantee that the replacement will be poor. His warning is about the possibility that people who are better equipped to make a decision may surrender their influence simply because they do not want the burden that comes with it.\nPlato’s view of power was more complicated than ambition\nPlato’s wider thinking makes the quotation more complicated than it first appears. He was not simply celebrating people who wanted to rule. In fact, his ideal ruler was not supposed to be motivated by wealth, prestige or personal power.\nIn The Republic, Plato imagined a class of philosopher-rulers who would be educated to understand justice and the wider interests of society. The person most suitable to govern might not be the person most eager to obtain authority.\nAmbition can make someone seek responsibility, but it does not prove that they are capable of handling it. A confident speaker may not be a good decision-maker. Someone who constantly seeks promotion may be less prepared for leadership than a quieter colleague with deeper experience.\nPlato’s concern was therefore not simply who gets power. Who is prepared to use it properly.\nHow failure to lead can become a problem\nAvoiding responsibility can sometimes be mistaken for humility. There is certainly value in recognising when another person is better suited to a task. A good leader does not need to be the best person at everything. Knowing when to listen, delegate or step aside can be part of sound judgement. The problem arises when reluctance has nothing to do with suitability.\nSomeone may refuse to speak because they fear criticism. They may avoid taking charge because they do not want to be blamed if things go wrong. They may watch a poor decision developing but remain silent because intervening feels uncomfortable.\nIn such cases, stepping back can become a form of disengagement.\nPlato’s quotation asks what happens afterwards. If a person capable of making a useful contribution refuses to do so, another person will still have to make the decision.\nWhat Plato’s philosophy says about good rulers\nThe quotation makes more sense when placed alongside Plato’s broader ideas about leadership. He believed that rulers needed education and a developed understanding of justice. Knowledge alone was not enough. A person also needed discipline and the ability to look beyond immediate personal interests.\nThis was very different from the idea that political leadership should simply belong to whoever could persuade the largest number of people.\nPlato had serious reservations about democracy as practised in ancient Athens, partly because he believed political decisions could be influenced by popularity rather than knowledge. His proposed alternative was highly theoretical and has been criticised for good reason, but it reflected a central concern running through his work.\nWhy leadership can be uncomfortable\nThe responsibilities attached to leadership are easy to underestimate. A person in charge may have to reject a colleague’s proposal, reduce a budget, change a plan or admit that a previous decision was wrong. They may have to make a choice despite incomplete information.\nThat can make avoiding leadership attractive. Someone who does not hold responsibility can observe a decision from the outside and point out what should have been done differently. The person making the decision does not have that luxury. They have to choose with whatever information is available at the time.\nThis is one reason Plato’s observation should not be treated as a simple celebration of authority. Leadership brings obligations as well as influence.\nThe question is whether the responsibility is worth accepting in a particular situation.\nWhat to do when you believe you can contribute\nPlato’s words can be applied without turning every situation into a competition for control.\nThe first step is to consider whether you genuinely have something useful to offer. Having a different opinion does not automatically mean having a better one. Experience, evidence and an understanding of the circumstances matter.\nIf you do have relevant knowledge, remaining silent purely because responsibility feels uncomfortable may deserve a second thought.\nThat does not necessarily mean taking command. It could mean raising an issue in a meeting, offering an alternative, volunteering for a difficult task or accepting responsibility for a project that needs direction.\nLeadership does not always begin with a title. Sometimes it begins with being willing to take responsibility for a decision.\nWhy the message still has relevance\nModern working life places considerable emphasis on individual achievement. People are encouraged to build careers, develop expertise and seek opportunities for advancement. At the same time, there can be an understandable reluctance to accept the risks that come with greater responsibility. The two can pull in opposite directions.\nSomeone may want their ideas to influence a decision without wanting to be accountable for the result. Another person may have the necessary experience but avoid senior positions because the additional pressure does not seem worthwhile.\nPlato’s observation provides a different way of looking at that choice. Influence and responsibility are often connected. If you want a meaningful role in deciding what happens, there may be occasions when accepting responsibility is part of the bargain.\nThat does not mean every leadership opportunity should be accepted. It means the decision to decline one deserves some thought.\nWhat the quote really teaches us about leadership\nLeadership is not simply about authority: Holding a position does not automatically make someone a good leader. Knowledge, judgement and responsibility matter.\n- Refusing responsibility can have consequences: Choosing not to participate does not mean decisions stop being made.\n- Ability and ambition are different: The person who wants power most is not necessarily the person best suited to use it.\n- Know when to step forward: If you have relevant experience or knowledge, there may be times when remaining silent allows a poorer decision to take shape.\n- Know when to step aside: Recognising that someone else is better prepared can also be a sign of good judgement.\n- Responsibility matters as much as influence: Having an opinion is easier than being accountable for what happens next.\n- Do not confuse superiority with competence: Plato’s use of “inferior” should not be treated as a judgement about a person’s worth. Different people have different strengths.\n- Leadership does not guarantee good outcomes: Taking responsibility does not mean every decision will succeed.\n- What matters is the reason for the choice: Stepping forward or stepping back can both be sensible, depending on the circumstances.", "link": "https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/world/europe/quote-of-the-day-by-plato-the-heaviest-penalty-for-declining-to-rule-is-the-ancient-lesson-about-choosing-who-leads/articleshow/133265252.cms", "date": "2026-08-16"}

{"title": "Iran's 134% food inflation bites hard: Meat, coffee and dairy quietly disappear from household tables", "content": "People in Iran have reportedly cut back on meat, dairy and coffee, among other food items, as pressure on household finances continues amid Tehran's prolonged war with the United States. Iran is struggling with a crippling economy, with hyperinflation mounting economic strain at home.\nMultiple reports have suggested that the war ruined tens of millions of households in Iran. \"Prices are up somewhere between 60 and 88% over the year, food has passed triple-digit inflation for the poorest households, and jobs - particularly full-time jobs and industrial work - are fewer,\" one of the reports claimed.\nAs the West Asia war seems to have no end in sight, here's what Iran's economy looks like as of now.\nIran’s year-on-year inflation rate remains above 80%, keeping pressure on household finances despite a decline in monthly inflation following recent currency and war shocks, ISNA reported on Saturday, 15 August.\nAt the end of July 2026, the Statistical Center of Iran (SCI) had recorded its fifth consecutive month of record annual inflation.\nIn a report released on 29 July, the Statistical Center put the 12-month inflation rate for the year ending in July at 66% for Iranian households, up from 62% in June. The SCI described it as the highest annual rate in decades.\nMeanwhile, data cited by Trade Economics, sourced from the SCI, showed that Iran's point-to-point/year-on-year inflation rate eased to 87.9% in July 2026 from 88.6% in June, marking the first slowdown in three months.\nHowever, the Central Bank of Iran recorded the twelve-month inflation at 61.4%, well below the SCI figure, according to NIAC insights. More than two-thirds of the food items monitored by the statistical agency now exceed what economists describe as crisis-level inflation, Iran International reported on 5 August.\nNot just food, but prices rose sharply across other sectors, the report added. Moreover, coffee consumption in Iran has also increasingly become an unaffordable luxury.\nAlthough global coffee prices declined, the cost of coffee beans in Iran — largely imported through the United Arab Emirates before the war — has nearly doubled compared to pre-war levels.\nThe increase directly affected café prices. {"title": "FinMin nudges ministries to switch to producer price index for rate adjustments in govt contracts", "content": "The finance ministry has nudged all ministries and departments to move to Producer Price Index (PPI), from the current Wholesale Price Index (WPI), for rate escalation and adjustment clauses in future government procurement contracts.\nThe Department of Expenditure, in a communication to all ministries and departments, said that PPI is a more internationally accepted index compared to WPI used in government contracts to define price escalation.\nFor the first time, the commerce ministry has started issuing monthly PPI data for both goods and services since June to better reflect price movement at the producer's level, thus paving the way for phasing out wholesale price inflation numbers in the next five years.\n\"Ministries/Departments are encouraged to adopt Producer Price Index (PPI) in place of Wholesale Price Index (WPI) in all price escalation clauses of future contracts, once PPI becomes available,\" the expenditure department said in an office memorandum dated July 13, which was sent to all ministries.\nThe price escalation or rate variation clause in government contracts allows payments to be adjusted in line with changes in the cost of key inputs, such as materials, labour and fuel, during the execution of a project. It helps distribute the impact of inflation between the government and the contractor.\nThe launch of monthly PPI data is in line with practices adopted by advanced economies and follows the recommendations of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which stressed that India needs to transition from WPI to PPI.\nThe output (goods) PPI cover all representative goods transacted in the economy. Manufactured items have the highest 69.93 per cent weight in output PPI (goods), followed by agriculture, forestry and fishing (22.16 per cent), electricity (4.49 per cent), and mining and quarrying (3.42 per cent).\nSeven services -- banking, securities transaction, insurance, management of pension funds, railways, air (passenger), and telecom -- have been covered in the first phase of Service PPI, while remaining services will be covered in the next phase, the Commerce and Industry Ministry had said while launching the PPI data in June.\nIn the case of Service PPI, no weights are being assigned, since the seven services does not cover the entire service sector.\nPublished on August 16, 2026", "link": "https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/economy/finmin-nudges-ministries-to-switch-to-producer-price-index-for-rate-adjustments-in-govt-contracts/article71352069.ece", "date": "2026-08-17"}
{"title": "From farm to bottle: How agriculture powers India’s beverage economy", "content": "India’s farms just delivered a record. The Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare’s Second Advance Estimates, released in June this year, put the country’s total horticulture production at 377.78 million tonnes for 2025-26, with fruit output alone rising 3.25 per cent to 121.48 million tonnes, led by banana, mango, papaya, apple and guava.\nNumbers like these tend to get filed under agriculture news and forgotten by the time anyone reaches for a juice carton. They shouldn’t be.\nEvery one of those tonnes is a potential input for an industry that spends most of its time talking about flavours, packaging and shelf space, and very little time talking about where its raw material actually comes from.\nThat is a mistake worth correcting, because the beverage business is, underneath the branding, a farm business wearing better clothes. A juice or RTD tea brand does not create fruit, sugar or water. It aggregates them, processes them and sells the result at a margin that depends entirely on how reliably those inputs show up. A record harvest is not a footnote for this industry. It is the year’s most important supply chain event, arguably more consequential than any single product launch.\nWhat a good harvest actually buys you\nThe temptation in a year like this is to treat abundance as permanent. It is not. Fruit output has grown for several years running, helped by government investment in irrigation, cold chain and processing infrastructure under schemes like Operation Greens, which now covers 22 perishables instead of the tomato, onion and potato it started with. But orchards do not scale the way factories do. A mango tree takes years to mature, a cold chain gap in one district can undo a season’s gains, and a single bad monsoon can reverse three years of steady growth overnight. The companies that treat a good year as licence to relax on sourcing relationships are the ones caught flat-footed when the next difficult one arrives. The companies that use a good year to lock in longer contracts, deepen farmer partnerships and invest in aggregation infrastructure are the ones still standing when it does not.\nThis is not an abstract concern. India’s non-alcoholic beverages market was valued at $14.95 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow at 7.36 per cent a year through 2030, according to the Ministry of Food Processing Industries. That growth will not be won on marketing spend alone. It will be won by whoever has methodically built the most dependable supply chain between farm and bottling line, because consumers are increasingly discerning about where a “real fruit” or “natural” claim actually comes from, and that scrutiny only grows as the market does.\nWater deserves the same long view\nThe same discipline applies to water, arguably more urgently. The Central Ground Water Board’s own data shows real progress here, with the share of India’s groundwater assessment units rated “safe” rising from 62.6 per cent in 2017 to 73.4 per cent in 2024. That is a genuine national achievement, built on years of recharge programmes and better monitoring. But a beverage company drawing from a single aquifer cannot afford to read a national average as a local guarantee. The responsible read of that improvement is not relief, it is a reminder that water stewardship has to be as deliberate and long-term as sourcing strategy, tracked block by block rather than assumed from the top line.\nFinal Thought\nNone of this makes for an easy headline. But the industries that will still be growing a decade from now are the ones treating agriculture as core infrastructure today, not as a line item to revisit when a harvest disappoints. This year’s numbers are good. What matters more is what gets built while they are.\nThe author is Joint Managing Director, SLMG Beverages\nPublished on August 16, 2026", "link": "https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/economy/agri-business/from-farm-to-bottle-how-agriculture-powers-indias-beverage-economy/article71346999.ece", "date": "2026-08-17"}

{"title": "How a private non-profit is fueling India’s sports medal tally", "content": "During his Independence Day address, Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressed India’s desire to host the 2036 Olympics in Ahmedabad, for which the country has already submitted a letter of intent to the organizers. The Olympic bid builds on the sporting and general infrastructure slated for the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad.\nAll of this puts India's sporting performance in the spotlight. At the recently concluded Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, India finished fourth with 39 medals. Nine of those medal winners were backed by Olympic Gold Quest (OGQ), a private company focused on helping Indian athletes win on the global stage. Notably, the organization's financial spending now surpasses even the government’s own funding for the same cause.\nPrivate bigger than public\nOGQ, officially named the Foundation for Promotion of Sports and Games, was established in 2001 by two of India’s sports legends: billiards champion Geet Sethi and badminton icon Prakash Padukone. It has identified 10 Olympic and 8 Paralympic sports in which India has a high chance of winning medals. It picks high-potential sportspersons from these sports, and supports them with coaching, equipment, travel to tournaments, and sports science.\nIn the past seven years, the scale of OGQ’s financial support has grown fourfold, from ₹19 crore in 2018-19 to ₹77 crore in 2024-25, clocking a compound annual growth rate of 26.2%. Its budget now exceeds the ₹34.8 crore spent by the government's parallel Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS). Over the same period, OGQ expanded its support from 82 to 178 senior athletes and increased its junior scholarship cohort from 81 to 110. Today, the foundation also backs 111 para-athletes, 3 sports federations, and 5 sports academies.\nDonors with heft\nBeyond cricket, Indian sports have traditionally relied on government backing due to a lack of commercial appeal. Winning medals elevates a sport's profile and opens up commercial opportunities, creating a virtuous cycle. While both OGQ and TOPS are chasing this goal, their strategies differ. TOPS casts a wider net—supporting 489 athletes leading up to Paris 2024 and 369 for Los Angeles 2028—but operates on a smaller budget, resulting in a lower average spend per athlete. At the Glasgow Games, TOPS supported 19 of India's 39 medallists.\nSportspersons can receive financial support from both programmes, as well as other corporate initiatives such as those run by the JSW Group or Reliance Foundation. Among these, OGQ stands out for its enterprise, structure, focus, and finances. It is entirely donor-funded, and the number of donors has more than doubled from 172 to 390 in the past five years. At the same time, the organization saw a decline in donors at the entry level ( ₹50,000 to ₹1 lakh), while donor numbers rose across all higher contribution tiers.\nSports and business\nIn the ₹1 crore and above tier, OGQ’s donor count expanded from 12 in 2020-21 to 31 in 2025-26. Equally impressive is the profile of these supporters, which includes leading corporates such as Axis Bank, Bajaj Group, three HDFC Group entities, HCL Group, Zerodha, and Delhivery, alongside philanthropies like the Rashesh Vidya Shah Family Foundation (associated with Edelweiss) and the HT Parekh Foundation (founded by HDFC's creator). Overall, OGQ presents as a well-funded, professional, and responsive organization.\nAt the same time, the foundation maintains its deep sports DNA. OGQ’s key promoters are former athletes, and its CEO—former Indian hockey star and passionate sports advocate Viren Rasquinha—earned a corporate-grade salary of ₹1.66 crore in 2024-25. That same year brought a shift in OGQ’s shareholding structure, as Shitin Desai (of DSP prominence) sold his 25% stake to chess legend Viswanathan Anand, Sameer Koticha of ASK Group, and Niraj Bajaj of the Bajaj Group. In 2024-25, OGQ's donation inflows surged from ₹68.9 crore to ₹92.1 crore.\nGovernment support\nPrivate initiatives like OGQ play a crucial role in India’s sports ecosystem. Outside of cricket, most national sports federations operate on tight budgets that cannot support grass-roots expansion, high-standard competitions, or competitive earnings for elite athletes. Demonstrating this funding gap, OGQ raised ₹92.1 crore in donations in 2024-25, exceeding the total combined income of six major Indian sports federations (shooting, athletics, wrestling, archery, boxing, and weightlifting).\nUnder-funded sporting federations are a global problem, and governments have to step in. A good example is the UK, which went from 15 Olympic medals in 1996 to 60-plus medals in each of the four Olympics starting London 2012. UK Sport runs a programme for elite athletes funded by the UK government and the National Lottery—a financial support system using money from ticket sales. Its budget was £100 million, or about ₹1,080 crore, in 2024-25. By comparison, India, which has averaged 5 medals in the last 4 Olympics, has a long way to go in providing financial assistance.\nEarning to spend\nThis was the chasm in support that Geet Sethi heard about at the 2000 Olympics and sought to bridge via OGQ. The organization’s impact is substantial: 13 of India's 21 medalists across the last four Olympic Games, and 33 of its 48 medalists over the last two Paralympic Games, received support from OGQ. Operating as a Section 8 non-profit company, its primary objective is to advance social welfare, making it eligible for tax benefits. Under this structure, all surplus funds remain within the organization and cannot be distributed to shareholders as dividends.\nIn each of the four financial years from 2021-22 to 2024-25, OGQ has spent at least 85% of its income for the year. Further, about 92% of its total expenditure in 2023-24 and 89% in 2024-25 was towards sportspersons, as opposed to its own staff or other expenses. The top five spending categories for athletes include travel, professional fees, lodging and boarding, equipment, and coaching fees.\nwww.howindialives.com is a database and search engine for public data", "link": "https://www.livemint.com/news/india/olympic-gold-quest-ogq-sports-india-2036-olympics-11786976316025.html", "date": "2026-08-18"}

{"title": "No State can block traditional routes of elephants: Supreme Court", "content": "The Supreme Court on Monday (August 17, 2026) directed the Centre to conduct a nationwide survey and take steps to ensure the free passage of wild elephant herds through their ancient corridors across States without human will or habitations blocking or impeding their natural routes.\n“No State can block their [elephants] paths. Blockading elephant corridors is not the solution to human-animal conflicts. Elephants travel across many States. One State cannot come in their way and block their traditional pathways. The solutions to this (animal-human conflict) are altogether different, and not constructing blockades,” Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said.\nJustice Joymalya Bagchi, on the three-judge Bench with Justice V. Mohana, said elephant pathways were not State-specific, and herds travel far by nature.\n“Elephant corridors have been obstructed, impeded, blocked due to some local factors. The Union of India must conduct a fresh survey and file a comprehensive report, which would include the necessary steps which were taken to prevent such obstructions,” Chief Justice Kant ordered.\nThe court directed the government to examine allegations that fireballs, mashaals (fire-torches) and spikes are thrown at wild elephants. In 2018, the apex court had prohibited the use of fireballs, burning rods, and spikes to chase elephants, calling them barbaric and illegal.\nThe court asked the government to ensure the implementation of the ban of such measures by ‘hula’ parties to drive away wild elephants from crops and villages. Elephants are Schedule I animals under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. They are considered a vulnerable species which receive absolute legal protection.\nAppearing for the Centre, Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati agreed to conduct a nationwide survey and submit the status report. Ms. Bhati sought three months, but the court said it would list the case after eight weeks to check on progress.\n“Construction of any kind of obstacle or creating blockades in elephant corridors is not acceptable. We are very clear that there cannot be obstacles in the way of wildlife. No State can say that just because crops are getting destroyed, they will have to construct obstacles on their path,” the Bench reiterated.\nJustice Bagchi said the practice of using fireballs and spikes was prevalent in West Bengal where the elephants came from Nepal and went to Jharkhand and other States. Chief Justice Kant said there were elephants in the Yamuna Nagar area of Haryana which travel to Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh.\nThe court was hearing a plea by advocate Shibani Ghosh, who submitted that fireballs continue to be thrown at wild elephants in West Bengal to drive them away from human habitation and croplands despite Supreme Court orders in 2018 to desist from the practice.\nPublished - August 17, 2026 05:21 pm IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/states-cant-create-blockades-in-elephant-corridors-sc/article71356053.ece", "date": "2026-08-18"}

{"title": "Ridding elections of black money is ECI’s responsibility: Supreme Court", "content": "The Supreme Court observed in a judgment on Monday (August 17, 2026) that ridding the electoral process from the influence of black money is a responsibility of the Election Commission of India (ECI).\n“Black money in the electoral process is one such aspect that compromises democracy, rule of law and the electoral process itself,” a judgment authored by Justice Sanjay Karol noted.\nBane of tainted money\nThe court said the bane of tainted money circulating and influencing voters’ choices was an age-old problem. It has been recognised time and again, but not yet resolved.\n“The choice exercised by the people once influenced by external factors is no longer a choice of their own. It is somebody else’s choice being thrust upon them. These external factors can take many shapes and forms... Ill-gotten, undeclared money is one of the primary forms used. It is this which is called ‘black money’,” Justice Karol observed.\nThe top court urged for timely investigations and conclusion of criminal cases relating to recovery of ill-gotten money during the elections.\nThe court cautioned that “any external factors that may influence this exercise of choice have the ability to compromise the very essence of democracy”.\nIt said the choice made by the individual is not free if ill-gotten money is involved and rather it is clouded by gratification, monetary or otherwise, or by promises sometimes genuine, other times misleading.\nCompromises electoral process\n“Black money in the electoral process i.e. the issue with which we are herein concerned, is one such aspect that compromises democracy, rule of law and the electoral process itself,” the Bench said.\nReferring to seizure of cash and assets during the election process, the Bench further said: “The authority affecting the seizure must, within 24 hours, report the same to the District Magistrate/Additional District Magistrate/Court having competent jurisdiction along with written reasons disclosing the prima facie nexus between the cash or other asset seized and the suspected electoral offence.”\nJustice Karol directed that when FIRs are registered, the investigation officer (IO) entrusted with the probe has to make every possible endeavour to complete it within a year. “If this timeline is exceeded, reasons therefore shall be recorded and communicated to the Election Commission of India,” the Bench pointed out.\nThe order was passed by the Bench on a plea filed by the Karnataka government related to the 2014 Lok Sabha polls, where large-scale black money was seized during elections in Bellary district.\nFile affidavit by Nov. 18\nAsking the Election Commission and State governments to file a compliance affidavit by November 18, the Bench directed the IO to submit a quarterly status report regarding the investigation to the electoral body.\nWhen Static Surveillance Teams find money in excess of ₹10 lakh during checks, information should be forwarded to the Income Tax authorities, the top court said.\nThe Bench directed High Courts to ensure speedy trial of election-related black money cases.\nPublished - August 17, 2026 11:04 pm IST", "link": Trump denied the allegation and repeatedly accused her of lying.\nThe case that resulted in the $5 million verdict focused on Trump's statements in 2022, when he described Carroll's allegation as a “hoax” and a “con job” on social media.\nA jury in 2023 found Trump liable for sexually abusing Carroll and defaming her, but it did not find him liable for rape, as Carroll had alleged.\nTrump paid nearly $5.63 million following the Supreme Court's decision in June, with the amount including the original $5 million judgment and interest, according to Reuters.\nCarroll's lawyer, Roberta Kaplan, welcomed Monday's decision.\n“We are pleased that the United States Supreme Court has declined again to hear this case,” Kaplan said.\n“As a result, the jury's unanimous verdict that Donald Trump sexually assaulted and then defamed E. Jean Carroll is now final and cannot be challenged in any court,” she added.\nSeparate $83.3 million Carroll case still before Supreme Court\nTrump still has another appeal before the Supreme Court involving Carroll. That case concerns a separate $83.3 million jury verdict over statements he made about her in 2019, while he was president.\nTrump and the Justice Department argue that presidential immunity protects him from Carroll's defamation lawsuit over those statements. The Supreme Court has not yet decided whether to hear that appeal.\nThe two Carroll cases are civil lawsuits and are separate from the Supreme Court's landmark 2024 ruling on presidential immunity in criminal cases. In that ruling, the court held that former presidents have absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for actions within their core constitutional powers.\nTrump has consistently denied Carroll's allegations and has maintained that the legal proceedings against him were unfair.", "link": "https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/world/us/us-supreme-court-again-rejects-donald-trumps-bid-to-overturn-5-million-e-jean-carroll-verdict/articleshow/133309489.cms", "date": "2026-08-18"}
{"title": "Taxing ‘frivolous’ industries will not fund India’s science", "content": "Whenever concerns are raised about the lack of funding for Indian science, a solution often put forward is to tax “unintellectual” industries such as cinema, tourism, apparel, and perfumes. For example, only recently, an academic from one of India’s leading research institutes suggested taxing the Indian Premier League (IPL), which, he argued, would magically generate “₹15 billion” for scientific pursuits; the “stroke of genius” was duly fawned over.\nThis reflects a common instinct: it is naturally hard not to want a share of the cake for a ‘nobler’ cause, when a ‘frivolous’ business makes profit in plain view.\nA flawed proposition\nIt is equally easy to overlook the economic cascade effects of such frivolities. Organised sport, for example, generates employment across a multitude of allied industries: merchandise, food and beverage, broadcasting, physiotherapy and rehabilitation (sports science is a science too). This investment has undeniable trickle-down benefits, across more sports than one and beyond major cities.\nThough well-intentioned, the myopic and fallacious “tax-this-to-fund-that” proposition needs to be dispelled immediately.\nIf ‘profit’ in the sports or film industries necessarily came at the expense of science, then the exercise in financial imputation should be very simple: of the $5 billion in profit earned by a match or a movie, $1 billion was made because a laboratory fell short of centrifuges. If that were true, then all scientists should refrain from watching movies or sports on government-subsidised campus Wi-Fi, as this would imply scientific funding flowing back to the entertainment industry. Luckily for them, the empirical evidence does not hold up: countries boasting a high expenditure on sport do not necessarily have poor scientific output, and vice versa. Besides, science is not an isolated pursuit: significant scientific input goes into making films or manufacturing textiles.\nThe disastrous economic experiments in India and around the world in the 20th century demonstrated that wealth is not a fixed, zero-sum pie: progress in X does not necessarily come at the expense of Y. As academics, we must refrain from making sweeping moralistic remarks, as though we know the right level of wealth surplus and how it should be spent better than the market does. Millions of dispersed individual decisions made by ordinary people contain more information than centralised academic or bureaucratic intelligence.\nMoreover, how do we know that the state can reliably direct the proceeds towards science? Government spending is the prerogative of bureaucrats and politicians, who are inevitably insulated from the consequences of such expenditure.\nShould the money be directed towards science, must it be distributed equally among all institutes and laboratories across the country, or apportioned according to productivity? If the latter, how will productivity be measured, and by whom? Some scientists appointed as advisers to the Department of Science and Technology? Would they not favour their colleagues and collaborators?\nBut, why only science? Just as scientists can make a fair claim for the setting up of state-of-the-art research laboratories, surgeons could demand better hospitals in Tier-3 towns, and policemen could call for better protective gear. Given the same pool of government money, how does one choose among these equally valid, competing claims? Politicians are notorious for basing such decisions on the electoral strength of each group, while academics form factions among themselves: microbiologists might grumble about theoretical physicists receiving disproportionately high funding, much to the delight of funding agencies.\nIf ‘only science’, then what kind of science? Should the money go towards buying more microscopes, gene sequencers, or chromatography equipment?\nMost scientists would, credulously, want these decisions to be left to scientists themselves: a grand delusion, for no subsidy is ever unconditional. A government that provides a fertilizer subsidy will ensure that it is used only to purchase fertilizers, and will go to extreme lengths to define what a fertilizer is. The subsidy giver has historically viewed the subsidy recipient as a potential embezzler. State funding for science is no different.\nWhat is ‘allowed’ instead of ‘needed’\nGovernment funding for science is, by definition, categorised into watertight compartments, for example, electronics, chemical reagents, consumables, travel grants, and equipment. Laboratories that do not need that extra bottle of hydrogen chloride but desperately need a computer monitor are often unable to make the purchase because the money has been rigidly earmarked. Once, a laboratory was allowed to purchase a server under “electronics”, but not a graphics card because, for some inexplicable reason, it fell under “consumables” rather than “electronics”. If a scientist does not spend all the money allocated to her in a financial year, she may receive less funding in the next one. This absurd incentive produces colossal wastage, as what is “allowed” is bought instead of what is “needed”, often at the cheapest possible price.\nConsequently, precious time is wasted learning tricks to circumvent these restrictions, much like companies did during the Licence Raj. Experiments are often put on hold while scientists navigate cumbersome procurement rules, particularly towards the end of each financial year.\nSteps to take\nTheoretically, the money is there, but it is squandered because its expenditure is predetermined by archaic rules that the bureaucracy has little incentive to change. Removing these restrictions would free up considerable resources for their intended use. Procurement aside, even the recruitment of scientists is governed by the archaic University Grants Commission Act (1956), contributing to India losing some of its best scientists to opportunities overseas.\nAnother indirect and “less bad” measure for expanding available funds would be to remove the Goods and Services Tax and steep import duties on scientific equipment. The rent on knowledge creation slows research and stagnates the circulation of money, which ultimately returns to the government.\nRight now, India also places crippling restrictions on private investment in science. Strict compliance requirements under CSR rules incentivise short-term, low-risk research projects. Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act procedures remain tedious, and many laboratories struggle to navigate the paperwork required to attract foreign funding. This is unfortunate, as private endowments have a greater stake in the success of research than any anonymous bureaucrat ever would.\nIn a bid to promote domestic manufacturing, the government has resorted to import substitution, a measure that serves only to insulate local industries from global competition while failing to deliver world-class products.\nThe mandatory adoption of the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) has been a death knell, further delaying procurement and forcing scientists to settle for cheaply made Indian equipment that looks identical on paper but falls short of international standards. Often, they spend time identifying “features” available only in foreign-made products so that they can be allowed to purchase them.\nIf a venture can be a great success in attracting international talent by virtue of being taxed less, so can other endeavours. For India to be at the forefront of science, the mechanism is to liberalise the bottlenecks through which money and capital somehow manage to trickle into academia and reduce dependence on the government, rather than taxing the few geese that lay the golden eggs.\nRitvik Chaturvedi is Senior Research Fellow, Centre for Earth Sciences, Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru. Website (www.ritvikc.com)\nPublished - August 18, 2026 12:16 am IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/lead/taxing-frivolous-industries-will-not-fund-indias-science/article71357138.ece", "date": "2026-08-18"}

Exciting to see what they can achieve.”\nMarijne later deleted the posts from both Instagram and X.\nFIH, however, responded to TOI’s request for clarification on what constitutes a dragging action during. “A dragging action occurs when the player moves the ball along the ground with the stick for a discernible distance before releasing it. This is characteristic of the drag component of a drag-flick and is not permitted when taking a penalty stroke,” FIH said in a reply to TOI.\n“The distinction is not determined solely by the length or shape of the stick movement. Umpires consider whether the ball is propelled from its stationary position as part of the push or flick, or whether it is first moved along the ground with the stick through a discernible part of the action before being released. {"title": "State Farm $5 billion dividend — Who qualifies for the payout and what customers need to know", "content": "State Farm has started distributing a one-time $5 billion cash-back dividend to eligible auto insurance customers, marking the largest such payout in the company's more than 100-year history.\nMillions of policyholders have already received their payments, while additional payments are expected to be sent in waves over the coming months.\nThe payout is a one-time policyholder dividend being distributed by State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company, the mutual company at the centre of State Farm's US auto insurance business.\nUnlike a conventional publicly traded insurer, a mutual insurance company is owned by its policyholders. State Farm says this structure allows it to return value directly to customers while maintaining the financial strength needed to meet future claims.\nThe $5 billion payout covers more than 49 million qualifying State Farm Mutual auto vehicles.\nCustomers with qualifying State Farm Mutual auto policies are eligible for the dividend.\nThe payment is calculated based on a percentage of the premium paid for each qualifying policy during 2025.\nThe percentage differs by state and ranges from 4% to 10%.\nThis means there is no single fixed payment amount for every customer. Someone who paid more in qualifying premiums could receive a larger dividend than a customer who paid less.\nIn simple terms:\nEligible 2025 premium × applicable state dividend percentage = estimated dividend\nFor example, a hypothetical customer who paid $2,000 in qualifying premiums and falls under a 5% dividend rate would receive about $100.\nThe actual amount depends on the customer's qualifying policy and applicable state percentage.\nState Farm is distributing the payments in waves, rather than sending all $5 billion simultaneously.\nBecause the programme covers more than 49 million vehicles, the company said the nationwide distribution will take several months.\nEligible customers will receive notification of their pending payment by email or letter. State Farm advises customers to watch for official communication regarding their dividend.\nThe dividend is separate from future insurance rates.\nState Farm said the payments are retrospective, meaning they are based on qualifying premiums paid in 2025 and do not directly determine future premiums.\nThe company said auto insurance rates are instead based on expected future costs and changing risk trends.\nState Farm also said the dividend comes alongside lower auto rates this year.\nState Farm said its mutual-company structure enables it to return value to policyholders.\nThe company's president and CEO, Jon Farney, said the payout reflects State Farm's customer-focused model while allowing the company to maintain financial strength.\nThe company described the dividend as part of its broader effort to provide value to customers.\nThe dividend distribution covers more than 49 million State Farm Mutual auto vehicles.\nState Farm said millions of customers have already received their individual payments, with additional payments continuing to be issued.\nBecause the dividend is calculated based on individual qualifying policies, payment amounts will vary from customer to customer and from state to state.\nCustomers with questions about their dividend can use State Farm's dedicated dividend resources.\nState Farm also directs customers to sfdividend.com or its Dividend Customer Contact Center at 1-888-808-9532 for payment-related questions.\nBecause the dividend programme involves millions of customers, policyholders should be cautious about unsolicited messages asking for sensitive financial or personal information.\nCustomers who receive a notification should verify that it relates to their State Farm policy and use State Farm's official channels for questions rather than relying on links or contact details in suspicious messages.\nOops! Notably, the non-oil-non-gold deficit alone increased to $55 billion in Apr-Jul FY27 from $42 billion last year.\nHowever, despite the widening merchandise deficit, the current account deficit remained contained at $6.2 billion in Q1, compared with a surplus of $1.2 billion a year ago, supported by a 9 per cent YoY rise in services exports to $52.2 billion and a sharp 34 per cent YoY increase in remittances to $41.4 billion.\nNotably, \"Remittance inflows seem to be front-loaded in Apr-May when as much as $29.5 billion of inflows were seen as against $11.9 billion in June,\" ICICI Bank noted.\nAt the same time, India's domestic demand is also expanding, and the recent rise in imports is likely to keep the goods deficit elevated. Based on current trends, \"goods deficit is estimated to increase to $390 billion in FY27,\" the lender noted.\n\"Assuming slightly lower oil prices in H2, goods deficit should be around $265 billion in the remaining eight months as against $237 billion last year (run-rate of $33 billion versus $30 billion last year),\" it said.\nHowever, FPI equity flows have reversed from $6.6 billion of outflows in the first fortnight of June to $5.4 billion of inflows since then.\nAt the same time, debt inflows have also strengthened to $7.3 billion, supported by changes in government securities taxation and a more positive outlook for the currency.\nWith India's prospective inclusion in the Bloomberg index, passive debt inflows are likely to remain strong even in FY28, as per ICICI Bank.\n\"The biggest change in capital flows is on account of FCNR inflows which have increased to $52.3 billion as of 13 August as against $36.7 billion as of end July,\" it stressed, adding \"overall BoP surplus for the year is estimated at around ~$55 billion which is positive for INR in the medium-term.\nOverall, as per the lender, in the longer term, the rupee outlook will depend on Asian currencies and capital inflows. However, renewed pressure on Asian currencies could create a depreciation bias for the Indian currency.\nPublished on August 18, 2026", "link": "https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/economy/indias-cad-may-widen-in-fy27-but-capital-flows-may-support-rupee-in-h2-report/article71358859.ece", "date": "2026-08-19"}
{"title": "Why is PM CARES Fund keeping large sums idle, asks RTI activist", "content": "The PM CARES (Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations) Fund received donations of ₹480 crore in 2024-25, down about 30% over the previous year, according to audited financial statements for 2023-24 and 2024-25 made available on Tuesday (August 18, 2026). Its total income, however, grew to ₹1,279.9 crore, up 41% over the previous year. The documents were released after a failure to upload annual disclosures since FY 2022-23.\nThe Hindu had highlighted the lapse on August 8.\nThe PM CARES Fund, a public charitable trust established in March 2020 to support relief efforts during public health emergencies and other disasters, is chaired by the Prime Minister and funded entirely through voluntary contributions, according to information released by the Union government.\nLimited spending\nReacting to the belated disclosure, Anjali Bhardwaj, co-convenor of the National Campaign for People’s Right to Information (NCPRI), said in a social media post: “Finally the audit statement of PMCARES Fund for 2024-25 has been made public! Key highlights — utilised only 0.01% of available ₹8,452 crore!”.\nMs. Bhardwaj was referring to the fact that, while the fund received a total of ₹1,279.9 crore in FY 2024-25 from net donations, interest on bank and fixed deposits, and refunds from implementing agencies, it spent only ₹87.85 lakh, which is 0.01% of the fund’s closing balance.\nFrom March 2020 to March 31, 2025, the fund has spent less than one-fifth (18.4%) of its total income.\nOpaque filings\nThe closing balance of PM CARES Fund stood at ₹8,452.06 crore in FY 2024-25, 17.8% higher than at the end of the previous year.\n“Why is the PM CARES Fund keeping such large sums of money idle,” Ms. Bhardwaj asked. She also noted that while ₹324 crore had been refunded by implementing agencies in 2024-25, no information was provided on the nature of these payments, reasons for the refunds, or the identity of the agencies involved.\n“Were refunds done to evade accountability for faulty equipment,” she said. “Also why have accompanying notes to the audit report not been uploaded?”\nLack of accountability\nMs. Bhardwaj said a fund set up to help citizens during disasters, which has accumulated thousands of crores including from foreign sources, is “shrouded in secrecy”.\n“Still no information available on sources of funds,” she said. “The PM CARES Fund continues to evade public scrutiny by refusing to submit itself to the RTI Act”.\nThe PM CARES Fund, established three days before the close of the FY 2019-20, has faced scrutiny over its transparency, following the absence of public audit statements after FY 2022-23. Critics have questioned why a fund — which accepts public money, including Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) contributions from public sector undertakings and donations from government employees — is made to seem like a public authority.\nThe Prime Minister chairs the fund in his ex officio capacity and Union Cabinet Ministers are its trustees.\n“However, when information regarding the funds collected and spent was sought, the government maintained that the trust is not a public authority under the RTI Act,” Ms. Bhardwaj told The Hindu. “The Ministry of Corporate Affairs also retrospectively amended the relevant rules under the Companies Act. At present, PM CARES remains outside the ambit of the RTI Act, parliamentary scrutiny and audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG).”\nPublished - August 18, 2026 05:31 pm IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/pm-cares-fund-audit-2024-25-domestic-foreign-donations/article71360330.ece", "date": "2026-08-19"}

{"title": "Ready to drop FIRs against student protesters, says Supreme Court", "content": "The Supreme Court on Tuesday (August 18, 2026) agreed to use an exceptional power under Article 142 of the Constitution to quash First Information Reports (FIRs) registered against students who joined nationwide protests over the NEET-UG exam paper leaks that led to the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan as Education Minister and compelled the government to introspect.\nAlso Read | NEET-UG protests: Listen to Gen Z, don’t repress them, says Supreme Court\nThe court sought a list of FIRs in which only students were named.\n“We will quash these FIRs by invoking Article 142. Protests in Delhi, which triggered agitations across the country, led to a police crackdown on July 20 in which pellet guns and tear gas were allegedly used.\n“But unless we have a list of these FIRs, how will we quash them,” Chief Justice Kant asked.\nSolicitor General Tushar Mehta, the government’s top law officer and Delhi Police counsel, said the police would confine their investigation to 2,873 persons with “serious criminal background” who were identified at the protest site. He said these persons included history-sheeters facing serious charges, including murder, rape, child sexual abuse, etc.\nJustice Joymalya Bagchi said the state cannot refer to “undesirable elements” in “generic” terms. “You have to at least identify them,” Justice Bagchi said.\n“We have identified 2,873. The rest are students,” Mr. Mehta responded.\nAdvocate Rizwan Ahmed, appearing for retired Air Force officer Manish Kumar Solanki, who has squarely blamed the organisers of the NEET-UG protests, including the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), for the July 20 violence, objected to the court’s proposed move to quash the FIRs against students. He asked if this would be a “one-off” or was the court setting a precedent. He said the students had not expressed a “shred of remorse or regret”.\n“The moot question here is whether the Parliament march was lawful or unlawful? The answer is, it is unlawful,” Mr. Ahmed submitted.\nSenior advocate N. Hariharan, on the petitioners’ side, said Mr. Ahmed seemed to ask the question and answer it as well.\n“The criminality of the protest has to be seen from the purpose for which the students were gathered there. Let us not forget their right under Article 19 [right to speech and dissent],” Chief Justice Kant addressed Mr. Ahmed.\nThe CJI said the court would protect the students “so long as they did not intend to violate the law, so long as they wanted to hold a protest in a peaceful and lawful manner and raise their voice with respect to certain demands which they expected the authorities to hear”.\nThe court said there was a clear distinction between cases involving peacefully agitating students and those against hardened criminals who infiltrated the protest to spread violence.\n“This is a question of the life and future of thousands of innocent students. Their parents spend hard-earned money for their education. They have a future. They have legitimate expectations from the system… We have to build up their confidence in the system. That is the real foundation,” Chief Justice Kant observed.\nThe Bench sought suggestions from petitioners for framing issues to be examined by the committee while noting that allegations of police officers sexually molesting women protesters would be looked into urgently by the panel for further legal action.\nSenior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, for the petitioners, said the Delhi Police affidavit did not spare a single mention about any internal or administrative action taken against police personnel allegedly captured on social media molesting women protesters.\n“The affidavit has an admission of plainclothes policemen present, without name tags. Once you start indulging in these kinds of disgusting activities, some responsibility should be put on individuals who are at the head of such chain of actions,” Mr. Sankaranarayanan submitted.\nSenior advocate Shadan Farasat asked why the state had not taken legal action against these police personnel.\n“We will frame issues which the high-powered committee proposed would go into. This would include issues the committee should go into urgently. The order would be out tomorrow,” the Chief Justice assured.\nMs. Grover, backed by Mr. Hariharan, said there ought to be a woman in the committee as the issues also concerned them.\nPublished - August 18, 2026 09:04 pm IST", "link": "https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/sc-ready-to-quash-firs-filed-against-students-for-neet-protests/article71360889.ece", "date": "2026-08-19"}

{"title": "India vs Pakistan Hockey World Cup: Knockout dream, survival at stake in blockbuster clash", "content": "NEW DELHI: The India-Pakistan rivalry returns to the FIH Men's Hockey World Cup stage on Wednesday with far more than bragging rights at stake. India need at least a draw to secure a place in the second round, while Pakistan must win the Pool D contest at the Wagener Stadium in Amstelveen to keep their campaign alive.\nIndia have three points from two matches after opening their campaign with a 3-1 win over Wales before suffering a 2-4 defeat against England. Pakistan, meanwhile, have one point after losing 1-4 to England and drawing 3-3 with Wales. England have already qualified for the next round after winning both their matches.\nThe high-pressure contest will also revive one of hockey's most storied rivalries at a venue steeped in its history.\nIndia hold the recent edge\nIndia will start as favourites given their recent dominance over Pakistan. They defeated their neighbours 7-1 and 4-3 during the European leg of the Pro League earlier this year, while Pakistan's last win over India came in the 2016 Champions Trophy.\nIndia have also won medals at the last two Olympics, while four-time World Cup champions Pakistan are returning to the tournament after an eight-year absence, having failed to qualify for the 2014 and 2023 editions.\nThe last World Cup meeting between the two sides came in Delhi in 2010, when India won 4-1. Pakistan subsequently missed the 2014 and 2023 editions and did not face India in the 2018 tournament.\nHowever, India's recent superiority will count for little once the two teams take the field. Pakistan have enough quality, particularly through their drag-flickers, to make the contest uncomfortable for India.\nIndia's most experienced player, Manpreet Singh, warned against complacency.\n“The match against Pakistan will be good, but we are not underestimating them. They also have good drag-flickers, so we will have to avoid giving them penalty corners. We must also create opportunities and capitalise on them. We must focus on our natural game,” Manpreet said.\nIndia will also be looking for a significant improvement in penalty-corner conversion after managing just one goal from four opportunities against England.\nPakistan have everything to play for\nPakistan's campaign has been uneven so far. They struggled against England before recovering to earn a 3-3 draw against Wales, but their defensive organisation and penalty-corner execution remain areas of concern.\nTheir preparations have also been far from ideal. Against England, their penalty-corner protection equipment was left in the dressing room, while they missed several opportunities against Wales before settling for a draw.\nPakistan captain Abu Bakar Mahmood believes the occasion will be decided on the day rather than by past records.\n“Rankings or past performance don't matter in a match between India and Pakistan. The team that plays well on match day will win, and we know how important this match is for our hockey, so we will leave no stone unturned,” he said.\nFor India, the equation is straightforward: avoid defeat and they progress. A win would guarantee second place in the pool. For Pakistan, anything less than three points will end their World Cup campaign.\nA historic venue for a historic rivalry\nThe Wagener Stadium adds another layer to Wednesday's contest. The venue hosted one of the most memorable India-Pakistan World Cup matches 53 years ago, when India edged Pakistan 1-0 in the 1973 semi-final.\nOn August 31, 1973, BP Govinda scored the decisive goal in the 62nd minute to send India into the final. The final was also played at the Wagener Stadium, with hosts Netherlands eventually beating India on penalty strokes after the match ended 2-2 following extra time.\nFormer India captain MP Ganesh, who was part of that side, still remembers the intensity of that semi-final.\n“It was one of the fittest Indian teams playing abroad.
